findings: Frontal chest radiograph. findings: Frontal (AP/portable) chest radiograph. findings: Frontal (AP, likely supine) chest radiograph with an 'L' marker. The cardiac silhouette is enlarged in appearance (manual cardiothoracic ratio about 0.59, range 0.59 to 0.65, inflated by AP magnification). Pulmonary vascular markings are indistinct/hazy, consistent with possible fluid overload. A left-sided central venous catheter is present with a coiled external segment over the left clavicle and the intravascular tip projecting over the SVC/cavoatrial region (appropriate position). Multiple ECG monitoring electrodes and an external IV infusion set are superimposed. No pneumothorax, no rib or clavicular fracture, and no endotracheal or nasogastric tube are identified.
impression: Portable AP chest radiograph showing bilateral basal opacities most consistent with atelectasis, consolidation, and/or pleural effusion (not separable on a single AP film), with possible superimposed pulmonary edema/fluid overload; the cardiac silhouette appears enlarged but true cardiomegaly is uncertain due to AP magnification. A left-sided central venous catheter is in appropriate position. No pneumothorax or acute bony injury.
limitations: Single portable AP view only (no lateral or PA comparison): AP projection and low lung volumes magnify the cardiac silhouette and limit cardiomegaly assessment. Overlying ECG leads and an external IV device obscure parts of the chest. The nature of the basal opacities (atelectasis vs consolidation vs effusion) cannot be definitively distinguished on one AP film. Pretrained pathology-classifier and zero-shot CLIP scores are second opinions with unreported single-image uncertainty, and the two classifiers disagree on cardiomegaly. The manual cardiothoracic ratio is limited by hazy cardiac borders and magnification. Clinical correlation is required.

findings: Supine/portable AP chest radiograph (L marker present). Diffuse bilateral airspace and interstitial opacities, patchy and reticulonodular, most prominent in the upper and mid zones, somewhat peripheral, with air bronchograms in areas of mid-zone consolidation; the lung bases are relatively more aerated, with a hazy left base (possible small left pleural effusion and/or dependent atelectasis, not definite). The cardiac silhouette appears enlarged (apparent cardiomegaly) and the mediastinum appears widened. A right-sided central venous catheter is present with its tip in the region of the SVC/right atrial junction (appears appropriately positioned). External ECG monitoring electrodes and wires overlie the chest. A large rounded subdiaphragmatic structure (liver/stomach) is seen below the right hemidiaphragm. No pneumothorax identified. No obvious acute osseous abnormality.
impression: Diffuse bilateral lung opacification with apparent cardiomegaly in a monitored patient (central venous catheter, ECG leads). Findings are most consistent with pulmonary edema (cardiogenic and/or non-cardiogenic, e.g. ARDS) and/or multifocal-bilateral pneumonia; the patchy, upper/mid-zone-predominant, somewhat peripheral pattern with air bronchograms does not fit classic perihilar cardiogenic edema, and a single supine AP view cannot definitively separate these — clinical correlation is required.
limitations: Single supine/portable AP view: overestimates heart size and obscures the diaphragm and costophrenic angles; no lateral view and no prior for comparison. External ECG electrodes/wires and the central line overlie and can mask lung markings. The edema-vs-pneumonia/ARDS distinction is not reliably made on one film: two supervised chest-XR classifiers (DenseNet121 and ResNet50, in agreement) score the pattern as diffuse infiltrate/pneumonia with edema low-to-borderline, whereas a zero-shot vision-language model (BiomedCLIP) favors edema; cardiomegaly is visually apparent but the classifiers' 'cardiomegaly' label is low (their 'enlarged cardiomediastinum' is present), and AP projection exaggerates the silhouette. The possible small left effusion/dependent atelectasis is uncertain. Model outputs are supportive only; all reported findings are visible in the original image.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (frontal projection confirmed). A right-sided double-lumen tunneled central venous catheter is present, with its luer-type connector/hub over the right lateral chest wall; the catheter courses through the superior vena cava and its tip projects over the SVC/right-atrial junction (appropriate position, no malposition). Multiple surgical clips/coils are seen: a cluster of about 4-6 in the right lower lung, several over the left heart border (suggestive of prior cardiac surgery), a small ring-shaped density in the upper mediastinum, and a small clip/marker crossing the catheter in the mid-mediastinum. A well-defined round soft-tissue opacity (approximately 1.5-2 cm) is present in the left mid-lung / left hilar region. An indeterminate faint lucency is noted at the right proximal humerus surgical neck. Both lungs are otherwise well aerated; no large pleural effusion, no pneumothorax, and no consolidation are seen, and there is no gross cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio approximately 0.5).
impression: Post-procedural chest radiograph: a right-sided central venous catheter in appropriate position and multiple surgical clips (status post cardiac and right-thoracic surgery), with no acute cardiopulmonary process. An indeterminate round opacity in the left mid-lung (vascular structure vs perihilar lymph node vs nodule) should be correlated with prior imaging or CT. No definite fracture is identified on careful review (the right humerus remains indeterminate).
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral view), which limits precise catheter-tip localization (the tip overlaps the spine/cardiac silhouette) and assessment of subtle findings (small pneumothorax, posterior effusion, and separating a hilar nodule from a vessel). A community bone-fracture model (no peer review) flagged 'fractured' (0.98), but this was not confirmed on careful visual re-examination (ribs intact; right humerus indeterminate), so a subtle fracture cannot be fully excluded. Pathology-model scores are operating-point (op_norm) values, not calibrated probabilities, and dense surgical clips can confound the nodule/mass scores. Zero-shot BiomedCLIP is phrase-sensitive and was used only as a soft second opinion. The image is a uint8 display PNG, so absolute intensities may differ from the raw DICOM. The right humerus lies at the field edge with limited resolution.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. A large, well-circumscribed, rounded, homogeneous soft-tissue opacity (mass) occupies the left mid-to-lower lung zone, abutting and partially obscuring the left heart border and the left hemidiaphragm, with a crescent of aerated lung around its lateral and superior aspect (consistent with an intrapulmonary location). The margins are smooth/rounded and slightly lobulated, with no spiculation, cavitation, air-fluid level, or calcification seen. The cardiac silhouette is normal in size (no cardiomegaly). The right lung is clear and well-aerated. The costophrenic angles appear sharp with no definite pleural effusion, and there is no pneumothorax. No second nodule or focal lesion is seen in the left apex.
impression: Large, well-circumscribed intrapulmonary mass in the left mid-lower lung, without cardiomegaly, effusion, or other acute finding. Tissue characterisation requires CT.
limitations: Single frontal projection only (no lateral view), so the exact depth of the mass and its relation to the pleura/mediastinum cannot be fully determined. No pixel-spacing or magnification metadata, so the mass size is reported only relative to the thorax, not in absolute centimetres. Large bilateral breast shadows overlie the lower lung zones, partially obscuring the inferior margin of the mass and the left costophrenic angle. The mass is fused with the heart/diaphragm on a single projection, limiting precise mass measurement. Tissue type (neoplasm vs hydatid vs infection) cannot be determined from a radiograph alone; CT is the appropriate next step. Pretrained-model outputs (view/pathology classifiers, PSPNet, MedSAM) are supportive but not definitive, and PSPNet was out-of-distribution for a mass of this size.

findings: Diffuse bilateral pulmonary opacification with a mixed interstitial (reticular / reticulonodular) and alveolar (mottled ground-glass, patchy) pattern; the right lung is more affected than the left, opacification is densest at the bases, and there is a focal patchy opacity in the right upper/mid zone. Both costophrenic angles are blunted/obscured by the basal opacity. The cardiac silhouette does not appear clearly enlarged but is partly obscured by the adjacent opacity. No pneumothorax and no definite focal pulmonary nodule or mass. No definite rib fracture. Multiple external metallic artifacts are present: maxillofacial dental work, two round ECG electrodes over the lateral chest walls, a small metallic device over the right shoulder, and a small mesh-like metallic device projecting over the mid-lower chest (left lower lung field).
impression: Diffuse bilateral pulmonary opacities with a mixed interstitial-alveolar (reticulonodular with mottled ground-glass) pattern, right greater than left, dense at the bases, with focal right upper/mid-zone accentuation. Most consistent with a diffuse infiltrative/inflammatory process such as multifocal pneumonia or pulmonary edema/ARDS; no clear cardiomegaly. Clinical and laboratory correlation is recommended.
limitations: Single frontal projection without a lateral view. Overlying external metallic hardware (dental, ECG electrodes, devices) obscures portions of the lung and confounds automated nodule/mass/fracture detection. Assessment of the cardiac silhouette is limited by adjacent opacification, so cardiomegaly can be neither confirmed nor excluded. The etiology of the diffuse opacification cannot be determined from a single radiograph (infection vs edema vs interstitial disease), and a small pleural effusion cannot be distinguished from basal consolidation/atelectasis. Pretrained model outputs were used as supporting evidence only; the bone-fracture classifier is out-of-distribution for chest radiographs and was not relied upon.

findings: Single frontal (AP/portable) chest radiograph. Diffuse bilateral pulmonary opacities with a basilar/mid-zone predominance and relative sparing of the upper lobes (right upper lobe most aerated). Dense, homogeneous opacity of the left lower hemithorax obscuring the left hemidiaphragm and left costophrenic angle (silhouette sign); differential for this left basilar opacity is pleural effusion, consolidation, or atelectasis. Coarse reticulonodular/patchy opacity in the right mid-lower lung zone. A right subclavian central venous catheter courses toward the SVC-RA junction (exact tip not precisely localizable due to overlying opacity; no obvious malposition). An implantable subcutaneous port with catheter is present in the right mid-chest wall. A second thin line overlies the patient's left upper zone (possible second central line or external lead). ECG skin electrodes overlie the chest. A small looped metallic density overlies the mid-cardiac region (curled catheter tip, retained guidewire, or external wire - indeterminate). The trachea is midline and air-filled; no endotracheal or tracheostomy tube is seen. No pneumothorax is identified at the apices. No displaced rib fracture is evident. The cardiac silhouette is partially obscured and its size is not reliably measurable on this AP projection.
impression: Diffuse bilateral pulmonary opacities, basilar-predominant with relative upper-lobe sparing, in a patient with central venous access. The leading considerations are pulmonary edema (cardiogenic or non-cardiogenic, e.g. ARDS) and/or bilateral pneumonia/infiltrate, accompanied by a dense left basilar opacity (effusion vs consolidation vs atelectasis). The specific etiology cannot be determined from a single frontal film and requires clinical correlation.
limitations: Single frontal projection only; no lateral view and no prior for comparison. Portable/AP, likely supine positioning exaggerates the cardiac silhouette and can mimic or obscure opacity; patient rotation and superimposed external devices (ECG electrodes, leads, port, central lines) limit assessment. The etiology of the bilateral opacities (edema vs infection) cannot be definitively established from one film. The dense left basilar opacity cannot be separated into effusion vs consolidation vs atelectasis without a lateral/decubitus view or further imaging. Cardiac size is not reliably measurable (AP projection, overlying opacity; an approximate cardiothoracic ratio of 0.62 from anatomy segmentation is overestimated). Pretrained-model limitations: the two pathology classifiers disagreed (DenseNet strongly positive; ResNet near-negative), and ResNet 'Lung Lesion' and 'Enlarged Cardiomediastinum' outputs were uncalibrated (NaN-threshold) defaults; model outputs were used only as supportive second-opinion readers, not ground truth; BiomedCLIP zero-shot scores were tightly bunched (low discrimination). The exact central-line tip position and the nature of the looped metallic density over the heart are not definitively established.

findings: Portable AP (frontal) chest radiograph of a critically ill patient, rotated, likely supine/semi-upright, with multiple external ECG monitoring leads/wires over both hemithoraces and a left-sided central venous catheter descending from the left neck; a black redaction bar obscures the right upper zone. There is bilateral airspace opacity/consolidation, right greater than left, densest in the right mid-to-lower zone where the right hemidiaphragm and costophrenic angle are obscured; the left lower zone is also hazy-opacified while the left apex is relatively clear. The cardiac silhouette is not clearly enlarged on this magnified AP view. No pneumothorax, no rib fracture, no discrete mass, and no subdiaphragmatic free air are identified.
impression: Bilateral (right-greater-than-left) airspace consolidation/infiltration, most dense at the right base, in a critically ill patient with a central line — most consistent with multifocal pneumonia/aspiration rather than dominant cardiogenic pulmonary edema (two independent classifiers score Edema and Cardiomegaly low and the opacity is asymmetric and basilar). A small right pleural effusion is possible but not definite, and superimposed edema cannot be excluded.
limitations: Single portable AP (frontal) projection, likely supine/semi-upright and rotated, which magnifies the cardiac silhouette, crowds the bases, and makes effusion vs consolidation difficult to separate. A black redaction bar obscures the right upper zone. Superimposed external ECG leads/wires and a central line partially obscure the lung fields. No lateral or PA comparison view is available. Pretrained models were trained mostly on standard PA chest radiographs, so their outputs are only partially valid on this cluttered AP film: the DenseNet 'Mass' score (0.77) was rejected as contradicted by the second model and by inspection, the PSPNet lung masks were partial/leaky (a spine-midline-based hemithorax measure was used instead for asymmetry), and the BiomedCLIP zero-shot similarities are not calibrated probabilities. Pleural effusion and superimposed edema cannot be definitively confirmed or excluded on this single film.

findings: Frontal upright chest radiograph. Confident findings: both lungs are well aerated and clear, with no focal consolidation, mass, nodule, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax; both hemidiaphragms are well domed and the costophrenic angles are sharp; the cardiac silhouette is normal in size (cardiothoracic ratio approx 0.37); the mediastinum, hila and trachea are unremarkable; a gastric air bubble is present; and the bony thorax (ribs, clavicles, spine) is intact with no obvious fracture or lytic/sclerotic lesion. No definite focal abnormality is visible. Uncertain observation: the lungs appear somewhat hyperlucent, so mild pulmonary hyperinflation / early emphysema is possible but not confirmed (the diaphragms are domed rather than flattened and classifier scores are borderline and discordant).
impression: Essentially a normal frontal chest radiograph with no definite acute abnormality; mild pulmonary hyperinflation is a possible but unconfirmed finding.
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral), so the retrocardiac region, subtle pleural disease, and the anteroposterior dimension of hyperinflation cannot be fully assessed. PA vs AP projection is not confirmed, which affects the cardiothoracic ratio and the apparent diaphragm position. The 1024-pixel resolution limits fine detail (small nodules, cortical margins). Pretrained model outputs were borderline and discordant (DenseNet121 weak positives vs ResNet50 clean); PSPNet segmentation was unreliable on this image and its quantitative outputs were rejected; the reticular texture seen with CLAHE enhancement was judged to be an enhancement artifact rather than true interstitial disease.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (likely AP/bedside), adult, probable female with bilateral breast shadows. A thin radiopaque tube/line runs from the right neck, down the right paramediastinum, across the chest, and down the left flank to the edge of the image; its course does not terminate in the stomach or the SVC, so it is not a correctly positioned enteric tube or central venous catheter - most consistent with an external tube/cable (e.g. monitoring lead or drainage tube) or a displaced enteric tube. External monitoring hardware is present: an ECG lead/electrode on the right neck, a small metallic clip at the left lateral chest wall, and an 'L' orientation marker; dental restorations are seen superiorly. The left lower zone/retrocardiac region shows increased opacity with adjacent gastric air, predominantly the superimposition of the left breast shadow and gastric gas with a hazy retrocardiac component; the right base is normal (aerated lung, smooth crisp hemidiaphragm, sharp costophrenic angle). The right hemidiaphragm is smooth and lies at a somewhat high position (about the 6th rib). A small faint midline radiopacity is seen at the upper thoracic spine (T1-T2), too small to characterize and not dense metal. No pneumothorax (apices and lateral margins clear with lung markings to the periphery), no obvious rib fracture, no obvious cardiomegaly, no large pleural effusion; trachea midline and mediastinum not widened.
impression: Frontal (likely AP) chest radiograph of a hospitalized patient with external monitoring hardware and a thin external/displaced tube. No definite acute cardiopulmonary abnormality is identified. The left-base/retrocardiac opacity is most likely superimposition (breast shadow plus gastric gas), with left lower lobe atelectasis or a small hiatal hernia not excluded on a single frontal view. No pneumothorax, rib fracture, cardiomegaly, or large effusion is seen.
limitations: Single frontal projection; PA vs AP cannot be distinguished (AP overestimates cardiac size and is associated with suboptimal inspiration) and no lateral view is available, so the left-base/retrocardiac opacity cannot be definitively characterized. Large breast shadows and superimposed gastric gas limit assessment of the left lower zone and left costophrenic angle. The image has a non-standard field of view (includes neck and upper abdomen) and external tube/metal, which cause artifacts and limit the reliability of the applied deep-learning models (domain shift); their outputs were used only as cross-checks. Source resolution (1024x1024) limits characterization of the small upper-thoracic-spine radiopacity. The tube's identity (external cable vs displaced enteric tube) cannot be determined definitively from a single image.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph of a monitored patient. A right-sided intercostal chest tube is present, entering via the right lower/lateral chest wall and curving superiorly with its tip in the right apex. The right apex is hyperlucent with reduced pulmonary vascular markings above the first rib. A second thin looped (pigtail-like) tubular device is seen in the right mid-to-lower lung zone. Patchy, reticular opacity is present in the right lower lung zone (atelectasis or post-surgical change). Multiple small metallic densities consistent with surgical clips are noted in the right lower lung and in a cluster below the left hemidiaphragm (left upper abdomen). Multiple external ECG monitoring leads/electrodes overlie the chest, and an external button/snap-fastener is seen over the left shoulder. The cardiac silhouette is within normal limits, the trachea is midline, the mediastinum is not clearly widened, and the costophrenic angles are sharp. No definite rib fracture is identified.
impression: Most consistent with a right (residual/partially drained) apical pneumothorax with a right apical chest tube in situ, in a post-surgical right hemithorax (surgical clips, right lower-zone atelectasis, pigtail-like drain) with prior left upper-quadrant surgery (clips), in a monitored patient. Note: no crisp visceral pleural line is visible, so the pneumothorax is the leading but not certain interpretation.
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral or second view); 8-bit PNG with flat exposure and black-corner letterboxing. Multiple superimposed external ECG leads and metallic devices can mimic or obscure a pleural line and a rib fracture. Because a chest tube and surgical clips alter the appearance relative to the pathology classifier's training data, the DenseNet-121 pneumothorax score is only borderline (op-norm 0.502, raw 0.014) and is not definitive. No crisp visceral pleural line is visible, so pneumothorax is a leading but uncertain interpretation. The exact nature of the looped right-lower device (intrathoracic drain vs looped external lead) is uncertain. Subtle rib fractures cannot be excluded on a single frontal view.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (view classifier: frontal 0.9996). Left hemithorax: a large collection of air without lung markings and a visible visceral pleural edge, with the left lung compressed medially - a large left pneumothorax (air occupies about 31% of the left hemithorax vs about 11% on the right). A chest tube (thoracostomy drain) lies in the left pleural space, and subcutaneous emphysema is present in the left lateral/axillary soft tissues. Right hemithorax: a moderate right pleural effusion (meniscus-shaped upper border) with basilar atelectasis/hazy opacity, obscuring the right hemidiaphragm and the right heart border. The trachea is approximately midline with no significant mediastinal shift apparent. No obvious rib or clavicle fracture. The inferior part of the image is saturated/over-exposed.
impression: Large left pneumothorax with a left chest tube in situ (no tension/mediastinal shift apparent) and subcutaneous emphysema, together with a moderate right pleural effusion and basilar atelectasis - a complex post-procedural/traumatic chest radiograph.
limitations: Single frontal view; no lateral, no prior for comparison, no clinical context. The inferior third is saturated/over-exposed, limiting assessment of the right costophrenic angle, diaphragms and upper abdomen. The tracheal air column is subtle, so a quantitative tracheal-deviation measurement was unreliable (no dramatic shift was seen on visual inspection). Pretrained classifiers were low-specificity on this extreme image (DenseNet121 positive on 14/18 labels; ResNet50 did not flag pneumothorax), so the pneumothorax rests on direct visual identification of the pleural line, supported by zero-shot BiomedCLIP and PSPNet air-fraction asymmetry. A community bone-fracture model (out-of-domain) strongly called 'Fractured' but this was refuted by direct bone inspection (likely a false positive from the chest tube).

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (likely AP/portable, supine). A large, dense, homogeneous opacity occupies the right lung base with a concave (meniscus-like) superior margin, obscuring the right hemidiaphragm and right costophrenic angle, consistent with a large right pleural effusion / hemothorax. A right-sided chest tube is in situ with its tip overlying the right base. There is extensive subcutaneous emphysema (streaky gas) tracking through the right axillary and lateral chest wall soft tissues. Multiple external ECG electrodes and lead wires are present, along with one or more additional thin lines (a central venous catheter tip could not be confidently identified). The left lung is relatively well-aerated with a sharp left costophrenic angle and only mild left lower-zone haziness. The mediastinum is wide and dense and the trachea appears near midline. No definite pneumothorax (no visible visceral pleural line or air-only zone), no definite rib fracture, and no gross tracheal deviation are identified on this view.
impression: Large right pleural effusion / hemothorax with a right chest tube in situ and extensive right subcutaneous emphysema (air leak) in a monitored patient; the combination is most consistent with a traumatic or post-procedural hemothorax +/- pneumothorax. No definite pneumothorax or rib fracture is visible on this single frontal view.
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral); likely supine/portable technique; an overall-bright (overexposed) image reduces contrast and limits detection of a subtle pneumothorax, a fine pleural line, and a rib fracture. The right arm is in the field and the extensive subcutaneous gas, chest tube, and ECG electrodes overlap the right hemithorax, limiting assessment of the right lateral chest wall and rib cage. The large right basal opacity and dense mediastinum obscure the right heart border, right hemidiaphragm, and tracheal/carinal anatomy. Automated pathology classifiers were out of distribution for this atypical image (arm in field, devices, subcutaneous gas) and were not relied upon for the findings. The exact etiology (traumatic vs post-procedural vs other) cannot be determined from the image alone.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. Dense, homogeneous opacity in the left lower zone (patient-left = image-right) that silhouettes/obscures the left hemidiaphragm and blunts the left costophrenic angle, extending from the dependent lower zone up into the left mid-lung. The right lung is clear with a normal right hemidiaphragm and a sharp right costophrenic angle. No cardiomegaly (cardiac silhouette within normal size). No pneumothorax. Trachea and mediastinum are midline (no obvious leftward shift). Normal gastric bubble. The film shows a slight tilt (about 2 degrees) and cropped corners.
impression: Left lower zone opacity, most likely a left pleural effusion and/or adjacent compressive basilar atelectasis; left lower lobe consolidation (pneumonia) cannot be excluded on this single frontal view. The dependent, homogeneous opacity that silhouettes the hemidiaphragm and blunts the costophrenic angle is the dominant finding. A lateral view and/or additional imaging (e.g., ultrasound or CT) would help confirm the nature of the opacity.
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral view), so the opacity's shape (meniscus vs wedge) cannot be confirmed, it cannot be localized as pleural vs parenchymal, and volume loss cannot be assessed. 8-bit PNG (no raw DICOM/Hounsfield values; fixed display window). The film is slightly tilted (about 2 degrees) and the corners are cropped (shoulders/lateral chest wall partly out of field). Model-based: the chest-XR classifiers disagree (DenseNet flags effusion/atelectasis, ResNet flags little); BiomedCLIP is a general vision-language model (lower reliability for a specific chest-XR label); PSPNet segmentation is coarse; MedSAM is box-dependent. No clinical context and no prior images for comparison.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. Dense, homogeneous right basal (right lower zone) opacity obscuring the right hemidiaphragm and the right costophrenic angle, with an ill-defined, roughly horizontal/slightly concave upper border (consistent with a right pleural effusion +/- associated basal atelectasis/consolidation). Right-sided indwelling drainage catheter(s): a pigtail (looped) catheter in the right upper zone and a thin, linear catheter/tube coursing along the right lateral chest wall from the mid-zone to below the diaphragm. Left lung is clear with a sharp left costophrenic angle and visible left hemidiaphragm. No pneumothorax; no definite cardiomegaly; mediastinum central and trachea midline. No rib fractures. Minor: faint patchy/interstitial markings in the right mid zone.
impression: Right basal opacity, most consistent with a (partially drained) right pleural effusion with associated basal atelectasis, in a patient with a right-sided pleural drainage catheter (pigtail/chest tube) in situ. Left lung unremarkable; no pneumothorax or cardiomegaly.
limitations: Single frontal view only; no lateral or decubitus view to definitively distinguish effusion from consolidation/atelectasis or to demonstrate fluid layering. 8-bit PNG export with limited dynamic range. The exact course and number of catheters cannot be fully determined on one frontal view (the pigtail loop and the long lateral line may be the same catheter or two separate catheters). AI model outputs are supportive only: the xrv classifiers and BiomedCLIP could not definitively separate effusion from consolidation/atelectasis, and the anatomy model's left/right labels had to be verified against the overlay. No clinical history or prior imaging available for comparison.

findings: AP portable chest radiograph of a monitored patient (external ECG electrodes and cables; two central venous catheters entering from the neck with tips projecting over the superior vena cava / brachiocephalic region; no endotracheal tube). There is dense, confluent opacification of the left lower zone and retrocardiac region, obscuring the left hemidiaphragm, the left heart border, and the left costophrenic angle. The lateral left mid-zone (upper lobe) remains relatively aerated and is separated from the opacity by a sharp oblique border; no definite air bronchograms are identified. The right lung is well aerated without focal opacity, and the right hemidiaphragm and right costophrenic angle are normal. The trachea is midline; no pneumothorax is seen. The cardiac silhouette cannot be fully assessed because of the AP projection and the left-sided opacity. Mild patient rotation is present.
impression: Large left lower lobe / retrocardiac opacity, most consistent with left lower lobe atelectasis (collapse), with left lower lobe consolidation (pneumonia) and a left pleural effusion (possibly coexisting) as the main alternatives. No pneumothorax. Bilateral central venous catheters are in appropriate positions.
limitations: Single AP portable (supine, rotated) view: magnification, rotation, and overlying monitoring hardware limit assessment of volume loss, mediastinal position, and cardiac size; the left heart border and left hemidiaphragm are obscured. Atelectasis, consolidation, and effusion can appear similar on a single frontal supine film, and their exact relative contributions cannot be separated; a lateral view and/or follow-up imaging would help. Pretrained model outputs were used only as corroboration: the two chest-X-ray classifiers disagreed on etiology, and a zero-shot vision-language model produced a false-positive endotracheal-tube finding that was excluded on visual inspection. This second-opinion interpretation does not replace clinical correlation.

findings: Frontal (AP/portable) chest radiograph. A large, rounded, homogeneous retrocardiac/left-base opacity with a smooth, well-circumscribed border is present, obscuring the left hemidiaphragm and the lower left heart border; no internal gas, air-fluid level, or air bronchogram is seen. The cardiac silhouette is enlarged (cardiomegaly), exaggerated by the AP projection. The right hemidiaphragm is elevated with a smooth contour and no free subdiaphragmatic air. A nasogastric/orogastric tube courses in the midline from the neck into the epigastrium, its tip in the stomach region. Three round radiopaque objects with attached wires (right chest, left axilla, epigastrium) are consistent with external ECG electrodes. Both glenohumeral joints are concentric with no dislocation or fracture. No pneumothorax or focal rib lesion is identified.
impression: Large rounded retrocardiac opacity with apparent cardiomegaly on a portable AP film. Most consistent with an enlarged, globular cardiac silhouette (cardiomegaly; pericardial effusion should be considered), with a hiatal hernia (no gas seen) and a left lower lobe collapse/consolidation or localized left pleural effusion as the main alternatives. A lateral view would help distinguish an enlarged heart from a retrocardiac hernia or mass.
limitations: Single frontal (AP, portable) view: magnifies the heart, and inspiratory effort, patient position (supine, large body habitus, raised arm) are suboptimal; no lateral view is available. The etiology of the rounded retrocardiac opacity cannot be definitively determined from one frontal image (enlarged heart vs hiatal hernia vs mass vs collapse). Pretrained model outputs were inconsistent and weak (pathology classifiers disagreed; PSPNet segmentation was anatomically unreliable on this image; the top BiomedCLIP prompt was contradicted by visual inspection), so model outputs were used only as weak supporting evidence and no finding rests on them alone. The tube tip is faint and its exact intragastric position could not be fully confirmed. The round objects are presumed external ECG electrodes but were not removed to confirm. The image is an 8-bit PNG export with mild top-clipping (max value 243).

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (PA or AP projection). Multiple small metallic surgical-clip densities are present in the right upper and mid lung fields, arranged in a curved arc, with an additional 2-3 clips over the right lateral chest wall and axilla. The right hemidiaphragm is elevated relative to the left, with a smooth convex dome-shaped contour at the right base and aerated lung above it. Both lungs are otherwise essentially clear, with no definite consolidation, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax. The cardiac silhouette is within normal size limits and the trachea is midline. No definite rib fracture or bony lesion is identified.
impression: Frontal chest radiograph demonstrating multiple surgical clips in the right hemithorax (consistent with prior surgery) and an elevated right hemidiaphragm (smooth dome). No acute cardiopulmonary process is identified.

impression: Multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules/masses with extensive right-sided subcutaneous emphysema and right chest tube in place. The overall pattern is highly concerning for metastatic pulmonary disease complicated by air leak requiring chest tube drainage. The extensive subcutaneous emphysema may also indicate associated pneumomediastinum.
limitations: Single frontal view without lateral projection. Assessment limited by extensive subcutaneous emphysema obscuring right-sided anatomy and overlying medical devices. The pretrained models (DenseNet, ViewModel, BiomedCLIP) showed limited reliability on this image due to the unusual presentation with extensive subcutaneous emphysema and medical devices — the ViewModel gave a wrong view classification, DenseNet missed the nodules, and BiomedCLIP scores were not well-calibrated. No prior imaging available for comparison.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph demonstrating bilateral pulmonary opacities, markedly asymmetric with right-sided predominance. The right lower lung zone shows extensive opacification obscuring the right hemidiaphragm and costophrenic angle. Patchy opacities are also present in the left lung, predominantly in the mid to lower zones. Multiple external ECG monitoring leads and wires overlie the chest. The cardiac silhouette appears enlarged but assessment is limited by AP projection. The trachea appears midline. No pneumothorax identified.
impression: Bilateral pulmonary opacities with marked right-sided predominance, consistent with multifocal pneumonia and/or ARDS. Right lower zone opacification with obscured costophrenic angle raises concern for concomitant right pleural effusion.
limitations: Single portable AP view with cardiac magnification and suboptimal lung expansion. Medical devices obscure anatomy. Pretrained models showed limited reliability (false-positive fracture, model disagreement). No lateral view available.

findings: Extensive right-sided alveolar consolidation involving the right mid and lower lung zones, with air bronchograms visible within the opacity. The consolidation obscures the right heart border and right hemidiaphragm (silhouette sign). Right costophrenic angle is blunted, suggestive of a concurrent pleural effusion. A chest tube is present, entering from the right lateral chest wall with its tip in the upper right hemithorax. The left lung is clear without focal consolidation, effusion, or pneumothorax. The left heart border is visible. The mediastinum is not widened. No acute bony abnormality is identified on this single view.
impression: Extensive right-sided alveolar consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with right middle and lower lobe pneumonia. Right-sided pleural effusion likely present. Chest tube in situ on the right. Left lung is clear.
limitations: Single frontal view only; no lateral view available to confirm extent of pathology or quantify effusion. Cannot definitively exclude concurrent pneumothorax given chest tube presence. Model-based scores (DenseNet, ResNet) are probabilistic and should not replace clinical judgment. The BiomedCLIP model could not be loaded for zero-shot classification, limiting the available evidence. Chest tube obscures part of the right lung field. Patient positioning and potential rotation may affect interpretation.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (likely AP view). Right-sided chest tube in situ with tip directed superiorly. Right apical and lateral pneumothorax with visible visceral pleural line and absent peripheral lung markings. Multiple right-sided rib fractures (at least mid-anterior ribs). Extensive subcutaneous emphysema tracking through the right chest wall and extending superiorly into the neck soft tissues. Right mid and lower zone patchy opacity, likely representing pulmonary contusion and/or atelectasis. Right hemidiaphragm elevated. No definite right pleural effusion appreciated. Left lung field clear. Cardiac silhouette appears mildly enlarged, though assessment limited by AP projection. ECG monitoring leads and wires overlie the chest.
impression: Right-sided pneumothorax with chest tube in situ, associated with multiple right rib fractures and extensive subcutaneous emphysema. Findings consistent with significant right-sided thoracic trauma.
limitations: Single frontal view without lateral projection. AP projection magnifies cardiac silhouette and reduces sensitivity for subtle findings. Extensive monitoring leads and chest tube obscure portions of the lung fields. Pretrained model scores (DenseNet, ResNet) had low specificity (0.5-0.7 range) due to presence of chest tube and monitoring equipment, and were used only as directional corroboration. Limited assessment of posterior ribs and full extent of subcutaneous emphysema without additional views.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (likely portable AP). Right apical pneumothorax with visible visceral pleural line and absence of lung markings in the right upper zone, despite a right-sided chest tube in place with its tip oriented toward the right apex. Heterogeneous opacification in the right mid-to-lower lung zones, suggestive of atelectasis and/or consolidation. Elevated right hemidiaphragm. Surgical clips in the right perihilar region, consistent with prior thoracic surgery. Multiple ECG monitoring leads overlying the chest wall. The left lung appears clear without focal opacity, effusion, or pneumothorax. No definite rib fracture identified, though assessment is limited by overlying medical devices and single frontal projection. Cardiac silhouette is within normal limits for an AP projection.
impression: Right apical pneumothorax with chest tube in place. Right mid-to-lower zone opacification consistent with atelectasis and/or consolidation. Findings are in the setting of prior thoracic surgery (surgical clips present). The pneumothorax persists despite chest tube placement, or the tube was placed after this image was obtained.
limitations: Single portable AP projection limits evaluation. Lateral view would improve assessment of retrocardiac opacities, pleural effusion, and anterior pneumothorax. The presence of a chest tube, ECG leads, and surgical clips creates superimposed artifacts. Rib fracture cannot be definitively excluded on a single frontal view without dedicated rib series. Clinical context and comparison with prior imaging would be valuable. Pretrained models (DenseNet, ViewModel, Bone-Fracture-Detection) were evaluated and found unreliable for this specific image. BiomedCLIP provided partial corroboration but zero-shot classification is inherently uncertain.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph demonstrates a dual-lumen central venous catheter entering from the right upper chest with its tip projecting over the right upper mediastinum. There is a significant right lower lung zone opacity with ill-defined margins, obscuring the right hemidiaphragm and right costophrenic angle. The opacity appears consistent with consolidation/infiltrate with possible associated pleural effusion. The right heart border is partially obscured. The left lung is clear except for a small linear opacity in the left lower zone, likely representing subsegmental atelectasis or scarring. The left costophrenic angle is sharp. The cardiac silhouette and mediastinal contours appear within normal limits.
impression: Right lower lobe consolidation/infiltrate with probable associated small right pleural effusion. In the appropriate clinical context, pneumonia is the primary concern. Differential includes atelectasis with superimposed infection. Linear opacity in the left lower zone is nonspecific, most consistent with atelectasis.
limitations: Single frontal view limits assessment of depth and localization of the opacity. Lateral view would help differentiate anterior vs posterior pathology. The presence of a central venous catheter may limit interpretation and affects automated model performance. Automated classification models (DenseNet, BiomedCLIP) provided supporting but not definitive evidence; DenseNet was unreliable with uniformly elevated scores. Clinical correlation and comparison with prior imaging are essential.

findings: Frontal (likely portable AP) chest radiograph of a monitored patient with bilateral ECG electrodes and external lead wires. Prominent bilateral breast shadows overlie and obscure the lung bases, hemidiaphragms and costophrenic angles. The visualized aerated lung fields are clear, without focal consolidation, mass, pneumothorax or large pleural effusion; pulmonary vessels are not markedly congested. The cardiac silhouette appears prominent, consistent with AP projection magnification and body habitus; an approximate cardiothoracic ratio (a lower bound of about 0.35, limited by segmentation of the peripheral lung fields) does not support true cardiomegaly. A thin, faint line in the right paramediastinum is consistent with an external ECG monitoring lead. No definite acute cardiopulmonary abnormality is identified.
impression: No acute cardiopulmonary finding identified. The apparent basilar opacity is explained by overlying breast soft tissue, and the apparent cardiac prominence by AP (portable) projection magnification. No consolidation, effusion, pneumothorax or mass is seen on this single frontal view.
limitations: Single frontal (likely portable AP) view; no lateral view. AP projection magnifies the cardiac silhouette and lowers the diaphragm, limiting assessment of heart size and the lung bases. Large bilateral breast shadows obscure the costophrenic angles, hemidiaphragms and true lung bases, so a small pleural effusion or basilar disease cannot be excluded. Overlying ECG electrodes, lead wires and external cables cast shadows that can mimic or hide findings. The image is a quantized 8-bit PNG with a limited dynamic range. Pretrained model outputs were used only as corroboration: the multi-label classifier operating thresholds are low (nonspecific lung-opacity/infiltration flags), the cardiothoracic ratio is a segmentation-based lower bound, and zero-shot CLIP was under-confident. A very faint internal line cannot be 100 percent excluded on a single frontal view.

findings: Single frontal (AP, portable) chest radiograph of a monitored, likely intubated patient. Multiple ECG electrodes/leads and wires are present, and a tracheal tube (endotracheal tube) is seen within the midline trachea with its tip at the mid-thoracic trachea (acceptable position, above the carina; no right mainstem intubation). The right hemithorax shows diffuse hazy increased opacity, most prominent in the mid-to-lower zones, with several rounded, thin-walled lucencies in the right mid-zone; the right hemidiaphragm and right costophrenic angle are not well identified (the right base is opacified). The left hemithorax shows hazy opacity in the left base/retrocardiac region with blunting of the left costophrenic angle. The cardiac silhouette appears enlarged (apparent cardiomegaly), accentuated by the AP/supine projection. A coiled metallic density overlies the left proximal humerus (indeterminate: external monitoring hardware vs orthopedic hardware), with no definite fracture line identified. No definite pneumothorax is seen.
impression: AP portable chest radiograph of a critically ill, monitored and intubated patient showing diffuse bilateral (right greater than left) pulmonary opacification, most consistent with a combination of pleural effusion, atelectasis and consolidation (with or without pulmonary edema). The rounded lucencies in the right mid-zone are most likely aerated lung / air bronchograms within the affected right lung; a bowel-related process (e.g. diaphragmatic hernia) is a less likely alternative that cannot be excluded on a single frontal view. Apparent cardiomegaly (projection-limited). Endotracheal tube in acceptable position.
limitations: Single frontal (AP) projection only; no lateral view and no prior study for comparison. Portable/supine AP geometry exaggerates the cardiac silhouette and lower-zone opacities and makes the hemidiaphragms and costophrenic angles harder to assess. Numerous external monitoring devices (ECG leads, wires, tracheal tube) overlie and obscure parts of the lung fields and confound the pretrained models. The image is 8-bit with limited soft-tissue contrast. The exact nature of the right-mid-zone rounded lucencies is indeterminate on a single frontal view (aerated lung/air bronchograms vs a bowel-related process); a lateral view and/or cross-sectional imaging would be needed to resolve this. The left-shoulder metallic density is indeterminate (external monitoring vs orthopedic hardware). Model outputs used here (pathology classifier, zero-shot, autoencoder, segmentation) are supporting evidence only and are confounded by the external devices and the unusual right hemithorax.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (PA/AP) of an adult female (bilateral breast shadows). Both lungs are well-aerated with no focal consolidation, mass, discrete nodule, pneumothorax, or pleural effusion. The cardiomediastinal silhouette is normal in size and contour with the heart within normal limits (no cardiomegaly) and the trachea midline. Both costophrenic angles are sharp and clear. A subtle linear (subsegmental) opacity is present in the left lower lung zone, most consistent with linear atelectasis (or a band of old scarring). The right hemidiaphragm sits slightly higher than the left, a normal anatomical variant. No acute rib, clavicle, or shoulder fracture is identified.
impression: Near-normal frontal chest radiograph with no acute cardiopulmonary abnormality. The only notable finding is a subtle linear atelectasis in the left lower lung, likely incidental and benign.
limitations: Single frontal projection only (no lateral view), limiting depth localization and assessment of the posterior costophrenic angles and diaphragm. The image is grainy/low-SNR, limiting detection of subtle parenchymal opacities. Breast shadows partially obscure the lower lung zones and cardiophrenic angles. Automated model outputs were weak or discordant: a borderline DenseNet 'Infiltration'/'Fibrosis' was not corroborated by the independent ResNet classifier or by visual inspection; the ResNet 'Lung Lesion'/'Enlarged Cardiomediastinum' scores are uncalibrated 0.5 placeholders (no operating threshold) and not true signals; and the cardiothoracic ratio is only an approximation because segmentation leaked to the image border. The linear opacity cannot be fully characterized (atelectasis vs. scar) on a single frontal view.

findings: AP (portable) chest radiograph of a young child. Marked cardiomegaly: enlarged, globular cardiac silhouette with a manually measured cardiothoracic ratio of ~0.66 (above the ~0.55 AP pediatric cutoff). Diffuse bilateral hazy / interstitial opacities, perihilar and mid-to-lower zone predominant, with indistinct, blurred pulmonary vessels - a pattern of interstitial pulmonary edema / pulmonary congestion. No focal dense consolidation, no large pleural effusion, and no pneumothorax are identified. Diaphragms are high (age/position) with a gastric air bubble present; no obvious free subdiaphragmatic air. Multiple external monitoring devices overlie the chest (ECG leads, snap electrodes, coiled wires, and a small round radiopaque device over the left upper abdomen / upper chest) - these are artifacts, not pathology. No rib or clavicular fracture is seen. There is mild patient rotation.
impression: Cardiomegaly with diffuse bilateral interstitial hazy opacities - a radiographic pattern most consistent with congestive heart failure / pulmonary edema, which in a child is most commonly due to congenital heart disease or cardiomyopathy.
limitations: Single portable AP/supine view with no lateral view and no prior comparison; AP geometry and supine position magnify the heart and can overestimate the CTR. Mild patient rotation. Overlying ECG leads/electrodes and wires partially obscure the lung fields and mediastinum. The patient is a small child, outside the adult training population of the pretrained models used as sanity checks; their outputs (including a spurious 'lateral' view call and divergent cardiomegaly scores) are uncalibrated here and were used only as corroboration, not as the basis of any finding. The etiology of the cardiomegaly/edema cannot be established from a single radiograph. The small round radiopaque object over the left upper abdomen is most likely an external device, but an ingested foreign body is not definitively excluded.

findings: Portable AP frontal chest radiograph of a monitored patient bearing multiple external ECG/monitoring electrodes and support lines. There is bilateral basilar opacification, greater on the right than the left: the right basal opacity is a homogeneous density extending up to the mid-chest with a smooth, gently convex superior border, and the left base is opacified to a lesser degree; both obscure the hemidiaphragms and costophrenic angles. The upper and mid lung zones are aerated; no pneumothorax is seen. The cardiac silhouette is prominent on this AP projection, but the manually measured cardiothoracic ratio is approximately 0.39 (below the 0.5 threshold), so the heart is not clearly enlarged; the prominence is largely AP magnification plus the adjacent basilar opacity. There are hazy perihilar markings that may reflect mild interstitial edema or infiltrate. The ribs, clavicles, scapulae and spine appear intact with no definite fracture, and no definite mass or nodule is identified. No free subdiaphragmatic air is seen.
impression: Portable AP chest radiograph showing bilateral basilar opacification (right > left), most consistent with atelectasis and/or small pleural effusion in a monitored, likely supine/bedside patient. The prominent cardiac silhouette is most likely due to AP magnification (cardiothoracic ratio ~0.39; no clear cardiomegaly). Possible mild pulmonary edema/infiltrate cannot be excluded. No pneumothorax and no definite rib fracture.
limitations: Single portable AP (bedside) projection, which magnifies the heart and mediastinum and reduces sharpness; the patient is likely supine/semi-recumbent, so effusions layer posteriorly, the diaphragms ride high, and the costophrenic angles are obscured. Numerous overlying external electrodes, wires and support lines obscure parts of the lung fields, and the intravascular position of any line cannot be determined from a single frontal image. The inferior cardiac border is lost in the basilar opacity, limiting accuracy of the cardiothoracic ratio (~0.39). Effusion cannot be reliably distinguished from atelectasis on a single frontal view. Pretrained models were used as supporting evidence only: the segmentation (PSPNet) was too noisy for quantitative CTR/diaphragm measurement, the zero-shot vision-language model (BiomedCLIP) had low discrimination, and some classifier labels (Lung Opacity, Mass, Fracture) were unreliable on controls or not visually corroborated. No PA or lateral view is available for comparison.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph. Bilateral, multifocal, patchy and hazy airspace opacities (infiltrates/patchy consolidation) are present, predominantly in the upper and mid zones of both lungs, most prominent in the right upper/mid-zone and the left perihilar/mid-zone, with relative sparing of the dependent lung bases. There is hazy retrocardiac (left lower lobe) opacity with partial obscuration of the left hemidiaphragm and left costophrenic angle. No definite pleural effusion (no meniscus), no pneumothorax, and no definite pulmonary mass or nodule. The cardiac silhouette appears widened but this is most likely AP magnification (no convincing cardiomegaly). A right-sided central venous catheter is present with its tip in the upper superior vena cava (appropriate position). A midline feeding/enteric tube passes below the diaphragm into the upper abdomen. ECG monitoring electrodes and external cables overlie the chest.
impression: Bilateral multifocal patchy/hazy airspace opacities consistent with multifocal/bilateral pneumonia (infectious infiltrate/consolidation), upper/mid-zone predominant. No convincing pulmonary edema, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, or mass. A small left pleural effusion cannot be excluded given the obscured left costophrenic angle.
limitations: Single frontal AP portable view only (no lateral view, no prior for comparison). AP geometry magnifies the cardiac silhouette (segmentation CTR 0.52 unreliable) and superimposes the scapulae over the apices. Superimposed external devices (ECG electrodes, central venous catheter, feeding tube) partially obscure the lung fields. The left hemidiaphragm/costophrenic angle is obscured by retrocardiac opacity and overlying soft tissue, so a small left pleural effusion cannot be excluded. No clinical context provided. Model support is limited: the xrv classifiers are trained mainly on PA-equivalent films (portable AP + devices are somewhat out-of-distribution), the two classifiers disagreed on consolidation/edema, MedSAM could not delineate the non-discrete infiltrate (documented negative), and BiomedCLIP is zero-shot and uncalibrated.

findings: AP (frontal) portable chest radiograph of a critically ill, intubated patient. Moderate-to-large LEFT pleural effusion: dense, homogeneous left basal/medial opacity with a concave (meniscus) upper border that obscures the left hemidiaphragm and the lower left heart border; the opacity is objectively much denser than the contralateral base and the ipsilateral upper lung. Right lung is aerated without pneumothorax, with only mild right basal haziness (mild atelectasis/effusion or positioning). Endotracheal tube lies in the trachea with its tip above the carina (approximately appropriate); central venous catheter(s) in situ; ECG monitoring electrodes on the chest wall. The patient is moderately rotated. The large radiolucent band on the left of the image is EXTERNAL air between the adducted right arm and the trunk (positioning artifact, not a pneumothorax or hyperlucent lung); a grid-like device over the left shoulder and a dense round object at the left shoulder are external monitoring hardware, not anatomy. The cardiac silhouette is not reliably assessable because of the AP projection, rotation, and the overlying left opacity.
impression: Intubated, critically ill patient whose dominant abnormality is a moderate-to-large LEFT pleural effusion, most likely with associated left lower lobe atelectasis and/or consolidation. The right lung is aerated with no pneumothorax; the endotracheal tube and central line are in acceptable position. No definite pneumothorax or other acute process is identified.
limitations: Single AP portable view (likely supine/semi-erect), with no lateral or prior comparison. Moderate patient rotation and AP projection distort the cardiac silhouette and tube positions and can mimic a mediastinal shift. The adducted right arm creates a large external air gap, and multiple external devices (ECG electrodes, shoulder hardware) overlie and obscure parts of the chest. The input is an 8-bit PNG with a fixed window and limited dynamic range. Pretrained chest-pathology classifiers (torchxrayvision DenseNet/ResNet) were degraded on this out-of-distribution image and did not corroborate the effusion, so their outputs were recorded as a negative result and not used to support any finding. The exact breakdown of the left opacity (effusion vs atelectasis vs consolidation) is uncertain, and cardiac size cannot be reliably assessed. Findings should be correlated clinically and, if the effusion is to be characterized or intervened upon, with repeat imaging or ultrasound.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph, rotated/oblique. Bilateral lower-zone (basilar) opacities, more extensive on the right (aerated lung extends only to the mid-lung) than on the left (basilar opacity). A left pleural pigtail drainage catheter is in situ over the left lower chest, the pigtail tip coiled, with the tube exiting the left lateral chest wall. Enlarged cardiomediastinal silhouette. Multiple external ECG monitoring leads and a thin left paramediastinal line (most likely an external ECG lead). Trachea patent, roughly midline. No pneumothorax, no acute rib fracture, no apical disease, and no discrete pulmonary mass or nodule.
impression: Bilateral basilar opacities (right more extensive than left) with a left pleural pigtail drainage catheter in situ and an enlarged cardiomediastinal silhouette on a rotated portable AP film - most consistent with bilateral pleural effusion(s) ± atelectasis/consolidation (± cardiogenic pulmonary edema), the left collection drained via the pigtail catheter.
limitations: Single rotated portable AP view with no PA/lateral view and no prior comparison; AP projection magnifies the heart and reduces penetration; supine/semi-upright positioning causes effusions to layer posteriorly (hazy basilar opacification) rather than form a meniscus, limiting separation of effusion from atelectasis/consolidation; overlying ECG leads and tubes can mimic or mask pathology; the cardiac silhouette blends with the adjacent opacities, limiting assessment of true heart size and the exact extent/laterality of the opacities; pretrained pathology-model scores do not laterlize and are sensitive to the overlying artifacts (used only as corroboration).

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. A right chest-wall implantable venous access port (reservoir) is present, with its catheter forming a prominent loop in the right upper chest and the tip projecting over the superior vena cava; a folded/redundant catheter segment is seen at the reservoir. Multiple surgical clips overlie the left mid-lung and left paracardiac region, and a small metallic clip is present in the left upper mediastinum. A cluster of 4-5 rounded soft-tissue opacities (approximately 1-2 cm each) projects over the right lower lobe, above the right hemidiaphragm. A rounded, somewhat prominent left hilar/perihilar opacity is noted. The cardiac silhouette is moderate (cardiothoracic ratio approximately 0.52, borderline). No pleural effusion, pneumothorax, or focal consolidation is identified; both costophrenic angles are sharp.
impression: Multiple rounded nodular opacities in the right lower lobe with a prominent left hilar opacity, in a patient with an indwelling port and prior surgical clips. Most concerning for multiple pulmonary nodules/lymphadenopathy (metastatic disease is a consideration given the port; granulomatous or inflammatory etiologies are also possible), warranting CT chest for characterization. No acute cardiopulmonary process (no effusion, pneumothorax, or consolidation).
limitations: Single frontal projection (no lateral view); PA vs AP is uncertain, affecting cardiac-size assessment (CT ratio ~0.52 is borderline) and characterization of hilar/mediastinal structures. The right-lower rounded opacity cluster cannot be definitively distinguished as pulmonary nodules versus mediastinal/pericardial lymphadenopathy on a single frontal view - CT is required. The catheter loop and the radiopaque band below the port reservoir are device-related and not fully characterizable (coiling vs malposition). 8-bit PNG conversion limits subtle low-contrast detail. No prior studies for comparison. Model-based pathology screening may be perturbed by the hardware; the PadChest-only variant over-called effusion/pneumonia that were not visually confirmed. Clinical history (e.g., indication for the port) is unavailable.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (frontal view confirmed with 0.994 model probability) of an adolescent/young-adult female. A well-defined, smooth, rounded soft-tissue opacity (approximately 4.5-5.5 cm) is present in the left perihilar/mediastinal region, forming a second contour on the left heart border with a sharp margin against aerated lung; segmentation and classifier evidence indicate it is separate from the cardiac silhouette and the heart itself is not clearly enlarged (approximate cardiothoracic ratio ~0.25, a lower bound). A small (approximately 1.2-1.6 cm) rounded opacity with a slightly lucent center is seen in the lateral left lower lung zone (small nodule vs bulla). A cluster of irregular metallic densities overlies the C2-C3 cervical region just below the mandible, with a pattern that could represent dental work or a metallic foreign body/retained fragments. The remaining lung fields are well aerated with no consolidation, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax; costophrenic angles are sharp; both hemidiaphragms are smooth with no subdiaphragmatic free air; the visualised bony thorax (ribs, clavicles, scapulae, spine) appears intact.
impression: Left perihilar/mediastinal mass. The dominant abnormality is a well-defined rounded soft-tissue mass in the left perihilar/mediastinal region that is distinct from a non-enlarged heart, in a young female. The leading differential is a mediastinal/perihilar mass (e.g. lymphoma, bronchogenic cyst, neurogenic tumour, thymic or germ-cell tumour); a vascular anomaly/prominent pulmonary artery is not excluded on a single frontal view. Secondary findings are a small left lower-zone rounded opacity and a cervical metallic density cluster (dental vs foreign body). CT of the chest is recommended to characterise the mass.
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral view), so the mass cannot be assigned to an anterior/middle/posterior mediastinal compartment and a purely vascular origin cannot be fully excluded. The patient is likely an adolescent/young-adult female, so adult reference values (e.g. cardiothoracic ratio, vascular sizes) do not fully apply. Pretrained-model outputs (DenseNet/ResNet pathology classifiers, BiomedCLIP zero-shot, PSPNet segmentation) are corroborating only, not diagnostic; the models were trained mainly on adult chest radiographs and the classifiers disagree in magnitude, and the PSPNet-derived cardiothoracic ratio is a lower bound due to heart-mask under-segmentation. The cervical metallic densities cannot be definitively classified as dental work versus a foreign body on this image. The input is a PNG re-save with fixed contrast.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. Bilateral diffuse reticulonodular and patchy airspace (interstitial-alveolar) pulmonary opacities, most marked in the mid and lower zones, partially obscuring the cardiac silhouette and the left hemidiaphragm. The left costophrenic angle is obscured by basilar haziness (a small pleural effusion or basilar atelectasis/consolidation cannot be excluded); the right costophrenic angle is relatively preserved. No pneumothorax. A 2x3 grid of metallic surgical clips is projected over the right mid-lung field (implanted hardware from prior surgery, not a mass). A mandibular reconstruction plate is present in the jaw region; ECG electrode markers are projected over both lateral chest walls; a small metallic clip is seen over the right shoulder. The cardiac silhouette is indeterminate (not clearly enlarged); the mediastinum is not widened; no endotracheal, nasogastric or central venous catheter is visualized. No displaced rib fracture is seen.
impression: Bilateral diffuse pulmonary opacities (reticulonodular/patchy interstitial-alveolar pattern), most consistent with pulmonary edema or multifocal pneumonia/infiltrates; a small left pleural effusion cannot be excluded. No pneumothorax. Multiple external monitoring devices and implanted hardware (mandibular plate, ECG electrodes, surgical clips) are present.
limitations: Single frontal view only - no lateral view and no prior images for comparison; 8-bit PNG without DICOM metadata (patient data, projection and exposure parameters unavailable). AP versus PA projection is uncertain (a view classifier confirms frontal but not AP/PA), which limits assessment of cardiac size, a finding further obscured by the diffuse opacities (cardiac silhouette indeterminate). Multiple superimposed metallic/external objects (mandibular plate, ECG electrodes, surgical clips, shoulder clip, corner marker) cause blooming and may obscure underlying anatomy; the surgical clips overlap the right lung field. The diffuse opacities themselves reduce contrast of the cardiac borders and costophrenic angles, so a small effusion cannot be definitively confirmed or excluded. Model-based readings are supportive but not definitive: DenseNet and ResNet disagree on fine-grained labels, BiomedCLIP is zero-shot and uncalibrated, and the metallic objects are partly out-of-distribution for these models (mitigated by a metal-suppressed re-run that left the scores unchanged). The distinction between edema and infection cannot be resolved from a single radiograph.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (likely AP/supine) of a hospitalized patient with multiple indwelling devices: a right-sided central venous catheter (looping, with a connector/anchor), a ring-shaped radiopaque device overlying the right mid-lung, a small surgical clip, and ECG electrodes. There are diffuse bilateral pulmonary opacities, most pronounced in the mid and lower lung zones, with a patchy interstitial-alveolar (consolidation) pattern that is asymmetric and most dense at the left base (near-complete opacification). Costophrenic angles are blunted/obscured (possible small pleural effusions). No definite pneumothorax, no discrete pulmonary nodule or mass, and no definite cardiomegaly (the cardiac silhouette is obscured by overlying opacity).
impression: Diffuse bilateral, lower-zone-predominant pulmonary opacities with a left-base consolidation in a patient with indwelling lines - most consistent with multifocal pneumonia (including aspiration) and/or pulmonary edema.
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral). Likely AP/supine projection, over-penetrated and low-contrast; multiple indwelling devices (catheter, ring device, clips, ECG electrodes) obscure the lung fields and mediastinum. The cardiac silhouette and costophrenic angles are obscured, so cardiac size and effusions cannot be reliably assessed. Pretrained model outputs (DenseNet/ResNet) were used only as corroboration of visible findings; Mass/Nodule scores and some threshold-pinned labels were discounted as device/threshold artifacts. The asymmetric (left > right) consolidation pattern favors pneumonia/aspiration, but pulmonary edema cannot be excluded.

findings: Portable anteroposterior (AP), supine chest radiograph of a monitored patient with multiple ECG electrodes, external monitoring cables, and a right-sided central venous catheter whose tip lies in the region of the superior vena cava. Diffuse bilateral airspace and interstitial opacities are present, more extensive on the right than the left, with basal and perihilar predominance and relative apical sparing; there is confluent consolidation in the right mid-to-lower zone with obscuration of the right heart border and right hemidiaphragm. The left mid-to-lower zone shows reticular and patchy airspace opacities with a hazy left base. No pneumothorax is identified and no endotracheal tube is seen. The cardiomediastinal silhouette is prominent, exaggerated by the AP projection; marked cardiomegaly is not demonstrated.
impression: Severely abnormal chest radiograph: diffuse bilateral airspace opacities in a critically ill, monitored patient, most consistent with severe acute bilateral lung disease - acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)/non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema versus severe multifocal pneumonia. Classic cardiogenic pulmonary edema is less strongly supported (no definite cardiomegaly, low model edema signal) but is not excluded. Right mid-lower zone consolidation with a possible small right pleural effusion.
limitations: Single portable AP supine view: magnifies the cardiac silhouette and reduces sensitivity for small pleural effusions and pneumothorax; dependent fluid layers posteriorly. Multiple overlying ECG electrodes and external cables and a redacted header degrade visualization of the lateral chest wall and right upper zone. Obscured lung bases prevent determination of whether a small right pleural effusion is present. findings: Frontal chest radiograph (frontal projection confirmed, 99.8%).
