findings: Frontal chest radiograph. Well-circumscribed rounded opacity in the left mid-lung zone, approximately 2-3 cm in diameter, with homogeneous density and smooth margins. No internal calcification or cavitation visible. No spiculation. Implanted venous access device (port-a-cath) in the right anterior chest wall with catheter ascending toward the superior vena cava. Multiple surgical clips projected over both lower chest walls, consistent with prior breast surgery. Cardiac silhouette within normal limits. Both hemidiaphragms normally contoured. No pleural effusion or pneumothorax. No acute bony abnormality identified. Lungs otherwise clear.
impression: Well-circumscribed rounded opacity in the left mid-lung zone. Given its homogeneous density, smooth margins, and lack of symmetry with the contralateral side, this is most consistent with a pulmonary nodule or mass rather than a nipple shadow. Clinical correlation and further imaging with CT chest is recommended for definitive characterization.
limitations: Single frontal view without lateral projection limits depth localization and characterization of the opacity. 8-bit image quality (PNG conversion from original DICOM) reduces dynamic range compared to original 12-bit radiograph. Pretrained model outputs (DenseNet-121) are supportive but not definitive, as the model was not trained with medical devices present in this image. BiomedCLIP zero-shot classification was non-discriminative for this image and did not contribute to interpretation. Nipple shadow cannot be completely excluded without a dedicated nipple marker view or CT.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph demonstrating a large, well-circumscribed, rounded opacity projecting over the left hilar region and left mid-lung zone. The opacity has smooth margins and homogeneous density, measuring approximately 6-8 cm in diameter. The normal left hilar anatomy is obscured and not separately identifiable. The right lung field is clear without focal consolidation, mass, or nodule. Both costophrenic angles are sharp without evidence of pleural effusion. The right heart border is visible; the left heart border is partially obscured by the opacity, making cardiac silhouette assessment limited. The trachea appears midline. No pneumothorax is identified. Bony thorax appears intact. Dental artifacts are visible in the upper image.
impression: Large well-circumscribed mass-like opacity in the left hilar/mediastinal region, most consistent with a prominent enlarged pulmonary artery segment (pulmonary artery aneurysm or markedly dilated main pulmonary artery) or a mediastinal mass. The smooth, rounded contour and location at the expected position of the left pulmonary artery favor a vascular etiology, though a neoplastic mass cannot be excluded on a single frontal radiograph.
limitations: Single frontal view without lateral projection limits characterization of the opacity's anterior-posterior location and precise anatomical relationship. CT angiography would be required to distinguish vascular from non-vascular etiologies. Pretrained classifiers showed variable agreement (DenseNet Mass 0.88 vs ResNet Mass 0.21), reflecting inherent uncertainty about the nature of the opacity. Bone-fracture detection model output was excluded as it was trained on wrist radiographs and is not applicable to chest imaging. The PSPNet segmentation model failed to identify the left hilar structure (0 pixels for Left Hilus Pulmonis class), likely due to the abnormality replacing normal hilar anatomy. BiomedCLIP zero-shot scores are not calibrated for diagnostic thresholds.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph demonstrating diffuse bilateral pulmonary opacities, more extensive in the left mid and lower lung zones and in the right upper and mid zones. The opacities appear patchy and somewhat confluent, with both airspace consolidation and interstitial components. Bilateral costophrenic angles are partially obscured, raising suspicion for small pleural effusions. The cardiac silhouette is partially obscured by the adjacent opacities, precluding accurate assessment of heart size. The mediastinum does not appear grossly widened. No pneumothorax is identified. No definite rib or clavicular fractures. External artifacts include a decorative necklace overlying the upper mediastinum and bilateral ECG electrode markers.
impression: Diffuse bilateral pulmonary opacities with both airspace and interstitial features, most consistent with multifocal pneumonia or interstitial lung disease. The extensive bilateral involvement with patchy consolidation favors an infectious or inflammatory etiology.
limitations: Single frontal view without lateral projection limits assessment of posterior opacities and pleural effusions. External artifacts (necklace, ECG electrodes) obscure portions of the upper chest and may mimic or mask pathology. Cardiac size assessment is limited by adjacent pulmonary opacities. Pretrained model analyses (DenseNet121) produced artifact-driven false positives and were deemed unreliable for this image. Zero-shot classification (BiomedCLIP) and single-pathology models (ResNet50) provide only supportive, not definitive, evidence. Clinical correlation and comparison with prior imaging are necessary.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph with multiple medical devices: port-a-cath implanted in the right chest wall with catheter coursing toward the superior vena cava, and multiple ECG monitoring leads overlying both hemithoraces. Dense opacity involving the left mid and lower lung zones with obscuration of the left heart border and left hemidiaphragm, consistent with a combination of consolidation and pleural effusion. Patchy bilateral airspace opacities are present in the right lung, less extensive than on the left. The cardiac silhouette appears enlarged, though accurate assessment is limited by AP projection. No pneumothorax is identified. The image is cropped inferiorly, limiting evaluation of the lung bases and costophrenic angles.
impression: Bilateral pulmonary opacities with left-sided predominance, most consistent with pneumonia with associated parapneumonic pleural effusion on the left. Possible component of pulmonary edema given bilateral involvement. Cardiac silhouette appears enlarged but cannot be reliably assessed on AP projection.
limitations: Single AP view without lateral projection limits assessment of cardiac size, posterior disease, and pleural fluid quantification. Image is cropped at the bottom, obscuring full evaluation of costophrenic angles and lung bases. Overlying monitoring equipment and medical devices obscure portions of both lungs. Pretrained model outputs (tXR DenseNet121) were partially trusted; high-confidence predictions consistent with visual findings, but moderate-confidence predictions (pneumothorax, fracture from community model) were not supported visually and disregarded. PSPNet segmentation was unreliable for this image and not used for interpretation.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph of a monitored patient with multiple ECG leads and a left-sided central venous catheter. Extensive right-sided opacity occupies the mid and lower lung zones with a gravity-dependent density gradient (progressively increasing from apex to base), obscuring the right hemidiaphragm, right costophrenic angle, and right heart border. The left lung demonstrates mild interstitial prominence with patchy opacity in the mid zone and a blunted left costophrenic angle. Cardiac silhouette assessment is limited by projection and adjacent opacity. No pneumothorax identified.
impression: Large right pleural effusion with overlying consolidation and atelectasis. Mild left-sided findings with possible small left pleural effusion and interstitial changes. Findings are most consistent with parapneumonic effusion or congestive heart failure with asymmetric right-predominant involvement.
limitations: Single portable AP view limits assessment of cardiac size and mediastinal structures. Overlying monitoring leads and redaction bar obscure portions of the image. No lateral view available to confirm effusion or characterize posterior anatomy. Pretrained radiograph classification and segmentation models failed due to normalization issues with this portable AP acquisition and could not be used as supporting evidence. Clinical correlation and comparison with prior studies recommended.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph of an intubated, centrally monitored patient. An endotracheal tube is in the trachea with a mid-tracheal tip (above the carina, not in a mainstem bronchus). A right-sided central venous catheter and multiple ECG monitoring leads are present. The right hemithorax shows diffuse hazy airspace opacity, greatest in the mid and lower zones, with air bronchograms and a dense basal opacity that obscures the right hemidiaphragm and costophrenic angle. The left hemithorax is relatively well aerated with only mild perihilar and peribronchial prominence. The cardiothoracic ratio is approximately 0.42, so the heart is not clearly enlarged. No definite pneumothorax, no subdiaphragmatic free air, and no displaced rib fracture are identified.
impression: Right-predominant hazy airspace opacity with air bronchograms and basal opacity, most consistent with a combination of atelectasis and pulmonary edema and/or consolidation (pneumonia or aspiration), with a likely associated right pleural effusion, in an intubated, supine ICU patient. The heart is not clearly enlarged and the visible devices are appropriately positioned.
limitations: Single portable AP projection with no lateral or prior comparison. Supine positioning magnifies the cardiac silhouette and allows free pleural fluid to layer posteriorly. Numerous superimposed devices (endotracheal tube, central line, ECG leads) obscure part of the field and image contrast is low. The cardiothoracic ratio is an approximation, so cardiomegaly cannot be definitively excluded. Pretrained models were trained mainly on upright standard radiographs, and this supine, device-laden film is at the edge of their training distribution; zero-shot (BiomedCLIP) similarity is not calibrated. Atelectasis, edema, and consolidation are hard to separate on a single projection. No clinical history or laboratory data are available.

findings: Frontal (AP, rotated) chest radiograph of a monitored patient. A central venous catheter enters via the right neck (right internal jugular) and descends through the superior vena cava toward the SVC/right atrial junction; the distal tip is not clearly identified. Multiple external ECG electrodes and monitoring cables overlie the chest and abdomen. The cardiac silhouette is enlarged (manual cardiothoracic ratio approximately 0.60-0.62) and hazy. Both lungs show increased hazy opacity, prominent perihilarly and in the lower zones (quantified as a symmetric lower-zone brightness increase of roughly 40-55% relative to the upper zones). No pneumothorax, no definite focal consolidation, no definite pleural effusion, and no rib fracture or other bony abnormality identified.
impression: Cardiomegaly with bilateral perihilar and lower-zone hazy opacities, most consistent with pulmonary edema/congestion, with dependent atelectasis likely contributing, in a patient with a right internal jugular central venous catheter and external monitoring. No definite focal pneumonia, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax.
limitations: Single frontal view; AP portable projection with leftward rotation (trachea offset about 47 px from thorax center, asymmetric hemithoraces) and low lung volumes, biasing the cardiothoracic ratio upward; image is hazy due to body habitus; external devices and cables partially obscure the lung fields; costophrenic angles and lung bases are obscured by body/breast shadows and cannot be fully assessed; central line tip unconfirmed; no lateral view or prior comparison available; pretrained model outputs were uncertain or discordant (DenseNet vs ResNet vs BiomedCLIP) and were used as supporting evidence only.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (adult; breast shadows visible). A thin, roughly horizontal linear (plate-like) opacity is present in the left lower lung zone, a few centimeters above the left hemidiaphragm, extending obliquely from the left cardiac border toward the lateral chest wall; it is intrapulmonary and feathered, most consistent with linear atelectasis. The cardiothoracic ratio measures approximately 0.52 at the widest heart level (borderline/upper limit of normal for a PA projection; indeterminate for AP). The remainder of the lungs is clear without focal consolidation, mass, pneumothorax, or pleural effusion; costophrenic angles are sharp. Trachea is midline and the mediastinal contour is unremarkable. Rounded lucencies near the right hilum are consistent with pulmonary vessels in cross-section. A small metallic-density external object is present in the left upper corner of the image, outside the body. No fracture or other skeletal abnormality is identified.
impression: Subtle linear (plate-like) atelectasis at the left lung base with borderline heart size; no other definite acute cardiopulmonary abnormality.
limitations: Single frontal view: PA versus AP projection cannot be determined, which affects the cardiomegaly cutoff and prevents confirming the plane of the left base linear opacity; no lateral view. The film is an 8-bit rendering whose data range tops out at 250, with dark detector corners and breast shadows attenuating the lower lung zones. A metallic external object in the left upper corner may confound whole-image model features. Pretrained outputs are global (non-localizing): the ResNet50 model has two untrained output labels (excluded), DenseNet/ResNet atelectasis signals are below operating thresholds, and BiomedCLIP zero-shot similarities are uncalibrated and were used only as supporting evidence. The CT ratio carries a measurement uncertainty of roughly +/-0.02.

findings: Frontal (AP, supine) chest radiograph of a young infant. Bilateral patchy airspace opacities, most confluent in the right mid and lower lung zones with air bronchograms, a rounded left upper lobe opacity with air bronchograms, and hazy increased density in the left lower zone. The cardiomediastinal silhouette appears wide; the measured cardiothoracic ratio is about 0.52 (upper bound 0.66), which is borderline on a supine infant film, and the right heart border is obscured by adjacent lung opacity. No pneumothorax and no definite pleural effusion. No internal device is seen. Multiple external monitoring artifacts overlay the image: ECG electrodes and lead wires over the upper chest, a probe with cable in the left upper quadrant, a tube along the left lateral body, a clip on the left lateral skin, and small metallic fragments in the left axilla; all lie on or outside the body contour.
impression: Multifocal patchy airspace disease with right mid-lung consolidation and left upper lobe involvement in a monitored supine infant, most consistent with pneumonia; cardiomegaly is not established (borderline CT ratio, likely AP magnification); no pneumothorax or definite effusion; all radiopaque objects are external monitoring equipment.
limitations: Single supine AP projection with no lateral view; the heart is magnified by the AP projection and the right heart border is obscured by adjacent lung opacity, so the CT ratio is an estimate (about 0.52, upper bound 0.66) and cardiomegaly cannot be confirmed or excluded; the infant chest is out of distribution for all adult-trained models used (the view classifier misclassified the full frame, the PSPNet masks failed the visual check, and the DenseNet121 and BiomedCLIP outputs showed strong non-content bias on sanity images), so no model output supports the primary findings; external ECG electrodes, wires and devices overlap the lung fields; the lower part of the image is overexposed, so the costophrenic angles and lung bases are suboptimally assessed; no clinical information (age, respiratory status) is available from the image.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph shows a large, ill-defined area of opacity in the right mid-to-lower lung zone. impression: Bilateral pulmonary opacities, most prominent in the right mid-to-lower lung zone, highly suggestive of pneumonia or consolidation. findings: The chest radiograph appears to be within normal limits. No acute findings such as pleural effusion, pneumothorax, or consolidation were identified.
Right lung mid-to-lower opacity; medical lines and tubes present in the thoracic cavity.
impression: Right lung consolidation.
limitations: Segmentation models (UNetResNet50, MedSAM) failed to provide useful anatomical localization; pathology scores from DenseNet121 were inconclusive.

findings: Large opacity in the right lower lung zone obscuring the right hemidiaphragm and costophrenic angle. Quantitative measurements show minimal tracheal deviation (2.5 mm, midline). impression: Large right-sided pleural effusion, potentially with associated underlying consolidation or atelectasis.
limitations: The precise nature of the opacity (effusion vs. consolidation) is difficult to definitively distinguish due to the extent of the opacity. Suboptimal lung volumes may affect the appearance of basal findings.

findings: Prominent, dense opacity in the left lower hemithorax obscuring the left costophrenic angle and diaphragm. impression: Large left-sided pleural effusion with associated compression atelectasis.
limitations: Single frontal view limits differentiation between effusion and primary parenchymal disease. Segmentation of left lung may be underestimated due to opacity obscuration.

findings: Frontal (AP portable) chest radiograph of a monitored patient with a right internal jugular central venous catheter and multiple ECG leads. The cardiac silhouette appears enlarged (cardiomegaly), though AP projection magnifies the heart. There is a left retrocardiac opacity obscuring the left heart border and left hemidiaphragm, with possible blunting of the left costophrenic angle. Patchy increased density is noted in the right lower lung zone. No pneumothorax is identified. Lung markings extend to the periphery bilaterally.
impression: Portable AP chest radiograph showing apparent cardiomegaly (partially projectional), left retrocardiac opacity (differential: atelectasis, consolidation, or pleural effusion), and patchy right lower zone opacity. Findings are concerning for congestive heart failure with dependent atelectasis, though infectious etiology cannot be excluded. Central venous catheter tip position appears appropriate. Clinical correlation and comparison with prior imaging recommended.
limitations: Single portable AP view limits cardiac size assessment (AP magnifies heart by 10-15%). Monitoring equipment (ECG leads, catheter) obscures portions of the lung fields. Left retrocardiac opacity cannot be definitively characterized as atelectasis, consolidation, or effusion without lateral view. Automated classifiers showed near-random output due to image normalization mismatch; PSPNet segmentation detected only 3 of 14 structures and is unreliable for this image.

findings: AP portable chest radiograph of an intubated critically ill patient with bilateral diffuse pulmonary opacities, significantly worse on the right (quantified: right lung mean intensity 92.9 vs left 120.0). The right costophrenic angle is obscured, consistent with pleural effusion. Retrocardiac opacity on the left suggests left lower lobe atelectasis or consolidation. The cardiac silhouette is prominent, though true cardiomegaly is uncertain given AP projection. Multiple medical devices are present: endotracheal tube, right-sided central venous catheter, ECG monitoring leads, and nasogastric tube. No obvious pneumothorax identified, though sensitivity is limited on AP portable films. Pretrained model concordance: DenseNet121 (all datasets) scores Lung Opacity 0.88, Effusion 0.71, Cardiomegaly 0.65; ResNet50 confirms Lung Opacity 0.90, Effusion 0.47; DenseNet121 (NIH) confirms Atelectasis 0.59, Cardiomegaly 0.58, Effusion 0.58.
impression: Extensive bilateral pulmonary opacification, right greater than left, with associated right-sided pleural effusion and left lower lobe atelectasis/consolidation in an intubated ICU patient. The pattern is consistent with a combination of airspace disease and pleural fluid accumulation. True cardiomegaly cannot be confirmed on this AP portable film.
limitations: Single AP portable view without lateral correlation; no prior imaging for comparison; multiple medical devices obscure portions of lung fields; AP projection magnifies cardiac silhouette; supine/semi-upright positioning causes dependent opacities; small pneumothorax cannot be excluded; no clinical context provided.

findings: Frontal (PA) chest radiograph of good technical quality. A linear horizontal opacity is present in the left mid-lung zone, most consistent with plate-like (discoid) atelectasis or subsegmental scarring. The cardiac silhouette appears within normal limits, though automated classification models assign borderline-elevated cardiomegaly scores (DenseNet121: 0.081, above calibrated threshold; ResNet50: Enlarged Cardiomediastinum 0.084, below threshold). Lungs are otherwise clear without focal consolidation, pneumothorax, or pleural effusion. Costophrenic angles are sharp bilaterally. Bony structures are intact without obvious fracture. PSPNet segmentation confirms normal anatomical structure localization. MedSAM successfully segments the left mid-lung linear opacity region. No focal anomaly detected by autoencoder reconstruction analysis. BiomedCLIP zero-shot classification was not available due to software incompatibility.
impression: Linear opacity in the left mid-lung zone, most consistent with plate-like atelectasis or benign scarring. No acute cardiopulmonary process identified. Borderline automated cardiomegaly score requires clinical correlation.
limitations: Single frontal view limits assessment of subtle findings that would benefit from a lateral view. Automated classification scores are generally low (<0.084), reflecting limited model confidence for this specific image. BiomedCLIP zero-shot classification failed due to open_clip 3.3.0 incompatibility with the model's HFTextEncoder architecture. Image resolution is 1024x1024 pixels, adequate but not equivalent to full-resolution digital radiography. Breast shadows limit lower lung zone assessment. CTR estimation from automated analysis was unreliable (estimated 1.00, actual likely <0.5).

findings: Frontal chest radiograph of a pediatric/infant patient in an ICU setting with multiple ECG monitoring electrodes and leads. Marked cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio 0.772), significantly above normal for AP projection. Diffuse bilateral pulmonary opacities with right-predominant involvement (quantitative zonal density: right mean 149 vs left mean 118, p<0.001). Left hemidiaphragm obscured; right hemidiaphragm partially visible. Costophrenic angles not clearly sharp.
impression: Critically ill pediatric/infant patient with severe cardiomegaly and diffuse bilateral pulmonary opacities (right-predominant), most consistent with congestive heart failure secondary to congenital heart disease, with associated pulmonary edema. Alternative considerations include severe bilateral pneumonia or post-operative cardiac status.
limitations: Single AP portable view of an 8-bit display-windowed image. No prior imaging for comparison. DenseNet/ResNet pathology classifiers trained on adult data showed all-18-positive pattern (out-of-distribution artifact) with only relative ranking being informative. BiomedCLIP could not be loaded. BiomedCLIP text encoder key mismatch prevented zero-shot classification. Clinical context (exact age, weight, respiratory support, cardiac history) unavailable.

findings: AP portable chest radiograph of a monitored patient. Dense left lower zone opacity obscuring the left hemidiaphragm and left heart border (silhouette sign). Less dense right basal opacity with possible right costophrenic angle blunting. Upper lung zones relatively clear. Cardiac silhouette appears enlarged, likely magnified by AP projection. Trachea midline. No gross fractures. Multiple ECG electrodes and a catheter/line in the left upper chest are present. No obvious pneumothorax visualized, though supine AP view has limited sensitivity for this finding.
impression: Bilateral lower zone opacities, significantly worse on the left, most consistent with bilateral pleural effusions (left greater than right) with associated compressive atelectasis and/or consolidation. Multiple monitoring devices in place, consistent with a critically ill inpatient setting. Pneumothorax cannot be excluded but is not visualized.
limitations: Single AP portable view limits assessment of cardiac size, opacity depth localization, and pneumothorax detection. Overlying monitoring devices obscure portions of the lung fields. No clinical context or prior imaging available for comparison. DenseNet121 and ResNet50 model outputs are supportive but trained primarily on PA erect films, creating a domain shift. True nature of left-sided opacity (effusion vs. consolidation vs. combined) remains uncertain.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (likely AP portable) showing bilateral diffuse patchy airspace opacities involving mid and lower lung zones, with lower-zone predominance confirmed by quantitative zone density analysis (upper/lower ratio 0.867). Symmetric involvement (left/right ratio 0.954). Left costophrenic angle is obscured, consistent with pleural effusion or consolidation. Right-sided peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) with tip in the expected SVC region. Multiple ECG monitoring electrodes and leads overlie the chest wall. Cardiac silhouette appears prominent but cardiomegaly assessment is limited by AP projection. ResNet-50 pathology classifier identifies Infiltration, Pneumonia, and Lung Opacity as positive; these three labels are agreed upon by both DenseNet-121 and ResNet-50. DenseNet-121 predicts 17/18 pathologies positive, but this reflects its very low calibrated thresholds rather than 17 coexisting pathologies. No pneumothorax visible on direct inspection.
impression: Bilateral diffuse patchy airspace opacities in a critically ill patient with monitoring equipment and central venous access. The pattern is most consistent with bilateral multifocal pneumonia, with cardiogenic pulmonary edema and ARDS as important differential considerations. Obscured left costophrenic angle suggests possible pleural effusion.
limitations: AP portable projection limits cardiac size assessment and may exaggerate vascular prominence. Clinical context (patient history, laboratory results, prior imaging) unavailable. Multiple monitoring devices obscure portions of lung fields. BiomedCLIP zero-shot classification unavailable due to model loading failure. DenseNet-121's broad positivity (17/18 labels) limits its discriminative value; ResNet-50's more conservative output (3/18 positive) is weighted higher. Single image without comparison to prior studies.

findings: AP portable chest radiograph of a critically ill patient. Multiple medical devices in situ: right-sided port-a-cath, ECG monitoring leads and electrodes bilaterally, central venous catheter, enteric tube, and external monitoring hardware. Bilateral pulmonary opacities are present, more extensive in the right mid-to-lower lung zone where the right heart border and right hemidiaphragm are obscured. The left lung shows patchy opacity predominantly in the lower zone, with the upper zone relatively more aerated. Costophrenic angles are not clearly delineated bilaterally, consistent with pleural effusions. The cardiac silhouette appears enlarged, though this assessment is limited by AP projection and patient rotation. No obvious pneumothorax is identified, though the evaluation is limited by patient rotation and overlying medical devices. The patient's right arm partially overlaps the right hemithorax. Trachea appears midline. Patient rotation is present.
impression: Bilateral pulmonary opacities on an AP portable film of a critically ill patient, with right mid-to-lower zone predominance. The findings are most consistent with a mixed etiology including pleural effusion and atelectasis, with possible superimposed consolidation. Cardiomegaly cannot be reliably assessed due to AP projection and patient rotation. Interpretation is significantly limited by patient rotation, extensive medical device overlay, portable AP technique, and incomplete costophrenic angle visualization.
limitations: AP portable projection limits cardiac and mediastinal assessment. Patient rotation (asymmetric clavicular positioning) further distorts anatomical relationships. Extensive medical device overlay (port-a-cath, ECG leads, central lines, external monitoring equipment) obscures significant portions of the lung fields. Costophrenic angles are not fully visualized, limiting pleural effusion assessment. No prior comparison studies available. Automated pathology classifiers (DenseNet-121 and ResNet-50) proved unreliable for this image due to out-of-distribution characteristics, producing contradictory results with 0/18 concordant predictions. Anatomical segmentation (PSPNet) failed entirely. Clinical context (mechanical ventilation status, fluid balance, infectious workup) would significantly aid interpretation.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph of an ICU patient with multiple medical devices including endotracheal tube, right-sided pigtail drainage catheter, ECG monitoring leads, and additional lines. No obvious pneumothorax is identified, though this is difficult to exclude on a single portable AP view. Image quality is limited by portable technique, patient rotation, and superimposed medical devices.
impression: Large left pleural effusion with associated atelectasis/consolidation. Right-sided pigtail catheter in situ. Endotracheal tube in place. Portable AP technique limits assessment of cardiac size, mediastinal shift, and subtle findings. Clinical correlation and comparison with prior imaging recommended.
limitations: Single portable AP view; no lateral or decubitus view available. Image rotation and supine positioning affect interpretation. Heavy medical device overlay obscures anatomy and confounds automated models. All pretrained models showed degraded performance on this image. Clinical context and prior imaging unavailable.

impression: Monitored adult patient with a properly coursing right internal jugular central venous catheter; prominent but not clearly enlarged cardiac silhouette (borderline CTR, likely magnified by AP projection); mild bilateral basilar atelectasis / low lung volumes. findings: Frontal chest radiograph, well-penetrated and well-inflated. findings: Frontal (AP) chest radiograph of a young pediatric patient (infant/young child) with external ECG monitoring electrodes and wires overlying the chest. findings: AP portable chest radiograph. findings: Frontal chest radiograph (likely AP/portable) showing bilateral, roughly symmetric, multifocal airspace opacities/infiltrates with lower-zone predominance (right mid-lower zone and left upper-mid zone, most confluent in both lower zones). findings: Frontal chest radiograph (left-side marker present). findings: Frontal (PA) chest radiograph. findings: Frontal chest radiograph of a small (pediatric) thorax, standard orientation (left laterality marker present). Bilateral diffuse reticulonodular and patchy alveolar opacities throughout both lung fields, most confluent in the left mid-lower zone, where the opacity silhouettes the left heart border and left hemidiaphragm; the right lung shows a coarse reticular network with patchy consolidation. Pulmonary edema (non-cardiogenic/ARDS more likely than cardiogenic, given no cardiomegaly) and a miliary or other diffuse infiltrative process are less likely but not excluded on this single view.

Superimposed metallic artifacts (dental prosthesis, ECG electrodes, and the indeterminate 2x3 metallic object) limit assessment and may confound automated models. findings: AP (portable) chest radiograph. findings: AP portable (supine) frontal chest radiograph with an 'R' marker. findings: Frontal (AP/PA) chest radiograph. The lungs are well-aerated and clear bilaterally, with no focal consolidation, no pleural effusion (costophrenic angles sharp), and no pneumothorax. findings: Frontal chest radiograph. findings: AP (anteroposterior) portable chest radiograph of a critically ill, intubated patient with multiple external monitoring electrodes and wires overlying the chest (external artifacts, not pathology). findings: Frontal (PA/AP) chest radiograph of a female patient: well penetrated, adequately inspired, and appropriately positioned (frontal projection confirmed). findings: Frontal chest radiograph (view classifier: frontal 0.999) of an adult with female body habitus (breast shadows). An implanted vascular access port (port-a-cath) is present in the right chest: a circular reservoir with a radiopaque chevron marker, its catheter ascending to the right apex, looping, then coursing medially through the mediastinum in the direction of the SVC; the exact catheter tip position cannot be determined on this single frontal film. A small (~3-4 mm), round, well-circumscribed calcified density is present at the right hilum, consistent with a calcified granuloma/lymph node. Both lungs are well expanded with no pneumothorax, no pleural effusion (both costophrenic angles sharp), and no focal consolidation or air bronchograms. The cardiac silhouette is within normal limits, the mediastinum is not widened, and the trachea is midline. No fracture of the ribs, clavicles, or the visible humeri or spine. Gas-filled bowel is seen below the right hemidiaphragm (normal). The mild left lower-zone density corresponds to overlap of the cardiac silhouette/diaphragm/gastric bubble rather than a focal opacity (confirmed by segmentation). A few indeterminate thin linear/rectangular radiopacities in the right lower abdomen (external artifact or clips).
impression: Frontal chest radiograph showing an implanted right-sided vascular access port (port-a-cath) and a small right hilar calcification, with no acute cardiopulmonary abnormality (no pneumothorax, effusion, consolidation, or cardiomegaly). No fracture identified.
limitations: Single frontal view only - no lateral/oblique views and no prior films for comparison; PA vs AP cannot be determined. The exact port catheter tip position cannot be established on a single frontal film. Image is 8-bit PNG with moderate contrast and a dense mediastinum, limiting assessment of the retrocardiac region and the catheter tip. A community bone-fracture model's 'Fractured' prediction was judged a false positive (its saliency was on the trachea/catheter/calcification, not bone; it is unvalidated and contradicted by direct reading and two chest-specific classifiers); a subtle non-displaced fracture cannot be absolutely excluded on a single frontal film. Zero-shot (BiomedCLIP) and community-model outputs were used only as corroborating evidence, never as sole support for a finding.

findings: AP (anteroposterior) portable chest radiograph. Support devices in situ: tracheostomy tube, intact median sternotomy wires, multiple ECG/monitoring leads, and a pigtail drainage catheter in the left lower hemithorax. Diffuse bilateral air-space/interstitial opacities, predominantly at the lung bases with the upper zones relatively spared. There is a dense right-basal opacity that obscures the right hemidiaphragm and right costophrenic angle (near white-out, with intensity approaching the cardiac silhouette), consistent with a moderate-to-large right pleural effusion with associated atelectasis/consolidation. The left lung base shows a milder hazy opacity around the pigtail catheter. No pneumothorax is seen at either apex or costophrenic angle. The cardiac and mediastinal silhouettes are difficult to assess on this AP supine film because of overlying opacities and sternotomy changes.
impression: Diffuse bilateral pulmonary opacities with basilar predominance — pulmonary edema (cardiogenic or non-cardiogenic) and/or multifocal air-space disease (pneumonia/ARDS) — together with a moderate-to-large right pleural effusion and a milder left-basal opacity, in a patient with a pigtail drainage catheter in the left lower hemithorax. No pneumothorax.
limitations: Single AP portable supine radiograph: cardiac and mediastinal size cannot be reliably assessed (magnification, rotation, and overlying devices/opacities). Pulmonary edema versus multifocal pneumonia/ARDS cannot be distinguished on imaging alone and requires clinical correlation and prior films for comparison. Pretrained model outputs are supportive, not diagnostic: the models were trained largely on PA films, so the AP/supine projection and overlying ICU devices (sternotomy wires, ECG leads, tracheostomy, pigtail catheter) are a distribution shift that can bias fine pattern discrimination, and the zero-shot BiomedCLIP similarities are directional only. The image is an 8-bit PNG export of unknown window/level. No lateral view, no prior comparison, and no clinical data were available.

findings: AP (likely portable) frontal chest radiograph. Hazy, ill-defined opacity in the left lower lung zone with bronchovascular markings still visible through it, abutting the left heart border and left hemidiaphragm; character indeterminate (atelectasis vs early/mild infiltrate, small effusion not excluded). Right lung base is clear (the opacity below the right hemidiaphragm is the liver). Upper and mid lung zones are clear without focal consolidation, pneumothorax, or obvious pleural effusion. Cardiac silhouette is moderately broad, likely exaggerated by AP projection; cardiomegaly not confirmed. External monitoring hardware is present: a thin lead crossing the right upper chest/shoulder and a coiled tube over the right lateral chest wall. No obvious rib fracture and no mediastinal widening.
impression: AP frontal chest radiograph showing a hazy left lower-zone opacity most consistent with atelectasis or an early/mild infiltrate; the remainder of the lungs is relatively clear. Cardiomegaly is not confirmed (AP magnification). External monitoring leads/tubing are present. No definite acute cardiopulmonary emergency (e.g., pneumothorax, large effusion) is identified.
limitations: Single frontal (AP, likely portable) view without a lateral; AP projection magnifies the heart, confounding heart-size assessment, and reduces lung detail. Lower lung zones are partly obscured by the diaphragm and overlying abdominal soft tissue, so the character of the left basilar opacity (atelectasis vs infiltrate vs small effusion) cannot be definitively distinguished. Pretrained models (DenseNet121, ResNet50, BiomedCLIP) were used only as corroborating evidence: they were over-sensitive (several borderline positives) and disagreed on cardiomegaly; the DenseNet 'Hernia' flag was not visually confirmed and was discarded. Anatomical segmentation (PSPNet) was misaligned on this image, so its cardiothoracic-ratio and intensity-profile measurements were discarded. External hardware limits assessment of the overlying region.

findings: Frontal (AP) portable chest radiograph, supine, in a monitored/intubated patient. Right hemithorax: a dense, homogeneous, confluent opacity in the right mid-to-lower zone that obscures the right hemidiaphragm and blunts the right costophrenic angle, with a curved, meniscus-like upper border (silhouette sign) and a reticular/patchy component in the right mid-lung; the right base is objectively more opaque than the left (measured zone asymmetry). Left lung comparatively aerated/clear. An endotracheal tube is present in the cervical trachea; a line descends from the left subclavian region toward the superior vena cava (central venous catheter vs ECG lead — indeterminate); multiple ECG electrodes and external cables overlie the chest. A white annotation arrow at the right lateral chest wall points at an external line/cable running along the body surface, with no definite acute intrathoracic finding at its tip. No definite pneumothorax (lung markings extend to the chest wall at the apex and laterally). Cardiac silhouette not clearly enlarged (supine AP overestimates size; approximate cardiothoracic ratio ~0.51). No acute bony abnormality identified on this non-bone-optimized view.
impression: Right base-predominant, homogeneous opacification most consistent with a right pleural effusion with associated atelectasis and/or consolidation (pneumonia), in a monitored, intubated patient; the left lung is comparatively clear. No definite pneumothorax or cardiomegaly.
limitations: Single supine portable AP view with no upright or lateral comparison, so a layering effusion cannot be fully characterized and effusion vs consolidation vs atelectasis cannot be definitively distinguished; the AP/supine projection overestimates cardiac and mediastinal size. Numerous overlying ECG electrodes and cables obscure the lung bases and costophrenic angles (especially the left) and limit assessment; there is some rotation/obliquity and arm overlap. Model-based outputs were unreliable on this image and were not used to establish any finding on their own: the view classifier mislabeled the projection, both anatomy segmenters degenerated, and the two pathology classifiers were discordant (one over-calling, one false-negative); interpretation rests on direct visual inspection, objective zone-intensity measurements, and a promptable segmentation (MedSAM) that tracked the opacity. BiomedCLIP is not chest-X-ray-specialized and was used only as supporting evidence. No clinical history or prior imaging was available for comparison, and the intended target of the white arrow annotation is ambiguous.

findings: Frontal (portable) chest radiograph. A pigtail-type chest catheter is in situ in the right hemithorax. There is extensive subcutaneous emphysema involving the neck, right chest wall, and axillae. The right apex is hyperlucent with a hazy right upper/mid-lung opacity; a right (apical) pneumothorax is suspected, though a discrete visceral pleural line is not clearly visualized. There is a well-circumscribed rounded opacity (~2-3 cm) in the left lower lung above the hemidiaphragm, and a patchy opacity in the left mid-lung. The cardiac silhouette is not enlarged and the mediastinum is not widened. Pneumomediastinum cannot be excluded.
impression: Right pneumothorax (likely partially drained) with a pigtail chest catheter in situ, accompanied by extensive subcutaneous emphysema, consistent with an air leak. Additionally, bilateral patchy opacities (atelectasis/consolidation) and an incidental left lower-lung rounded opacity (nodule/mass vs rounded atelectasis) requiring further characterization.
limitations: Single frontal (portable) view; no lateral view, no prior films for comparison, and no clinical history. A discrete visceral pleural line was not identifiable, so the size and residual extent of the right pneumothorax are uncertain; the right apex is obscured by the catheter and overlying opacity. The left lower rounded opacity cannot be definitively characterized (nodule vs atelectasis) on a single radiograph and warrants CT or follow-up. AI-assisted model outputs (DenseNet, ResNet50, BiomedCLIP, PSPNet, MedSAM) were used only as supporting, non-definitive evidence and are not validated for this specific presentation. Pneumomediastinum cannot be excluded on a single frontal view.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph (frontal view). Bilateral pulmonary opacities, predominantly in the mid-to-lower zones and more confluent in the right lung: the right mid-to-lower lung shows patchy airspace opacity with air bronchograms and obscuration of the right hemidiaphragm, while the left mid-to-lower lung shows mottled, reticular airspace opacity with the left upper zone relatively spared. The right costophrenic angle is blunted/obscured, suggesting a possible small right pleural effusion. Low lung volumes. Multiple EXTERNAL monitoring devices overlie the chest: a ring-shaped device over the left mid-lung, a hook-shaped clip over the mid-chest, ECG electrodes at both shoulders, and lead wires. The cardiac silhouette is poorly delineated and the mediastinum appears widened (largely AP projection). No pneumothorax, no obvious rib fracture, and no traceable malpositioned tube/line are identified.
impression: Bilateral airspace/parenchymal opacities (right greater than left) in a monitored/inpatient patient, most consistent with multifocal pulmonary disease (multifocal pneumonia or pulmonary edema/ARDS). Possible small right pleural effusion. No confident cardiomegaly, pneumothorax, or fracture. The specific etiology cannot be definitively determined on a single portable AP film.
limitations: Portable AP projection (mediastinal/heart magnification, scatter, under-penetrated bases), patient rotation, and overlying external monitoring hardware that obscure the lung fields. The image is an 8-bit PNG render without DICOM metadata, so windowing is empirical; only a single frontal view is available (no lateral). The pretrained view classifier mislabeled this frontal film as 'Lateral' (distribution shift) and that output was discarded. The three pathology classifiers agree that opacities are present but disagree on the specific etiology and on cardiomegaly, so model outputs were used only as weak supporting evidence. The etiology (infection vs edema vs ARDS) and the presence/size of a pleural effusion cannot be definitively determined on a single film.

findings: Frontal (likely AP) chest radiograph. There is an extensive right-sided (patient's right) airspace opacity involving the mid and lower zones, which is mottled and multifocal and contains air bronchograms, consistent with consolidation. The right heart border and the right hemidiaphragm are obscured. The left lung is clear. There is no pneumothorax, no definite cavity, no definite rib fracture, and no mediastinal shift. A thin radiopaque line, most consistent with an external monitoring lead or a thin catheter, overlies the right hemithorax. A gastric bubble is present.
impression: Large right-sided (right middle and lower lobe) airspace consolidation, most consistent with pneumonia. The left lung is clear. A small accompanying right pleural effusion cannot be excluded.
limitations: Single frontal view only; no lateral view to separate parenchymal from pleural disease or to localize anterior vs posterior. 8-bit PNG without DICOM metadata (fixed window, no HU values). The right hemidiaphragm and right costophrenic angle are obscured by the opacity, so a small accompanying effusion cannot be excluded. The cardiac silhouette is partially obscured, limiting assessment of cardiac size. The superimposed thin line (external lead or thin catheter) partly overlies the affected lung. Pretrained model outputs were cross-checked across multiple models; the bone-fracture classifier was out-of-domain and its output was not relied upon.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph of a monitored patient. Multiple thin external ECG monitoring lead wires and electrode snaps overlie the chest and upper abdomen; no endotracheal tube, nasogastric tube, central venous catheter, or chest drain is identified. There is a patchy, ill-defined opacity in the right mid-lower lung zone with possible air bronchograms, partially obscuring the right hemidiaphragm and the adjacent right heart border; the right costophrenic angle is partly obscured. The left lower zone is mildly hazy/reticular but still aerated, clearly less extensive than the right. Both lung apices are well-aerated with no pleural line. The cardiac silhouette is not obviously enlarged and the mediastinum is central. No pneumothorax, no obvious pulmonary edema, and no definite rib or skeletal fracture are seen. A normal gastric air bubble is present beneath the left hemidiaphragm.
impression: Predominantly right-sided patchy right mid-lower zone opacity, most consistent with consolidation/infiltrate (pneumonia) with or without atelectasis; a contributing small right pleural effusion cannot be excluded. The left base is only mildly affected. No pneumothorax, no cardiomegaly, no pulmonary edema.
limitations: Single frontal projection only (no lateral view for exact lobar localization); 8-bit PNG export without DICOM metadata (reduced bit depth, unknown exposure/technique, AP vs PA uncertain); external ECG lead wires and electrode snaps overlap the lung fields and may mimic or obscure pathology; the lower zones are partly obscured by the hemidiaphragms and overlying devices; calibrated pathology-model scores are supporting reference only and showed cross-architecture disagreement on this atypical image; the BiomedCLIP zero-shot result is supplementary only; no clinical history is available.

findings: Portable frontal (AP) chest radiograph. A right-sided chest tube (drain) is in situ, entering at the right apex and coursing down the right hemithorax. There is a large, homogeneous, dense opacity occupying the right lower hemithorax with a roughly horizontal upper margin that rises laterally (meniscus), obscuring the right hemidiaphragm and the right heart border; the right upper zone remains aerated. Multiple small metallic surgical clips/staples are seen in the right paratracheal/perihilar and upper mediastinal region. The left lung is well aerated and clear with a sharp costophrenic angle. External ECG monitoring electrodes and wires overlie the chest and abdomen (artifacts). No definite pneumothorax is visible, and no subdiaphragmatic free air is identified.
impression: Large right pleural effusion (hydropneumothorax not excluded) with a right chest tube in situ, in a post-procedural/post-surgical patient (surgical clips in the right paratracheal region). The left lung is normal. No definite pneumothorax or pneumoperitoneum is visible.
limitations: Single frontal view (no lateral). 8-bit PNG with compressed dynamic range (no native DICOM/PACS windowing). Portable AP technique with overlying ECG electrodes and a chest tube, which limits regional assessment. Patient position (upright vs semi-recumbent) cannot be confirmed, which affects the appearance of the fluid level and the distinction between a meniscus and a flat air-fluid level. Pretrained pathology classifiers were unreliable on this image (two models disagreed and clustered near the operating threshold); BiomedCLIP strongly supported only the chest tube, so findings rest primarily on direct visual inspection.

findings: Single frontal chest radiograph. A hazy, patchy opacity is present in the right mid-to-lower lung zone, obscuring the right hemidiaphragm, partially silhouetting the right heart border, and blunting the right costophrenic angle. A central venous catheter is in situ: two parallel radiopaque lines enter from the right upper thorax with a loop in the proximal course, and the distal tip(s) project over the superior vena cava to cavoatrial junction region. No visceral pleural line is identified (no pneumothorax). The cardiac silhouette is not definitively enlarged, though the right heart border is obscured by the opacity. The mediastinum is of normal width. The left lung is clear and the left costophrenic angle is sharp.
impression: Most consistent with right lower lobe pneumonia (consolidation), possibly with atelectasis and a small right pleural effusion. In-situ central venous catheter with tip in the SVC/cavoatrial region and a proximal loop. No pneumothorax and no definite cardiomegaly.
limitations: Single frontal projection only (no lateral view), so the exact nature of the right-base opacity (consolidation vs effusion vs atelectasis) and the presence of a small effusion cannot be definitively separated. The lung apices are partly cut off by a black band at the top of the image, and the image is soft/grainy with a non-uniform background. The right heart border is obscured by the opacity, limiting assessment of heart size. Whether the catheter is a dual-lumen catheter or two adjacent catheters cannot be definitively resolved on a single frontal view. Pretrained pathology scores (DenseNet/ResNet) are calibrated operating-point values (0.5 = threshold), not probabilities, and can be influenced by the catheter and the dark image corners; a DenseNet 'mass' score was discounted as a false positive on cross-model and visual disagreement.

findings: AP portable chest radiograph of a critically ill patient with extensive monitoring equipment (tracheostomy tube, ECG leads, monitoring wires). Dense homogeneous opacity in the left lower lung zone obscuring the left heart border and left hemidiaphragm (positive silhouette sign). Patchy consolidative opacity in the right mid and lower lung zones. Both costophrenic angles are not clearly sharp, left worse than right. Cardiac silhouette appears enlarged, though AP projection magnifies heart size. No definite pneumothorax visible, though evaluation is limited by overlying devices.
impression: Bilateral pulmonary opacities, left greater than right, most consistent with multifocal pneumonia (ventilator-associated or hospital-acquired) with associated left pleural effusion and dependent atelectasis. Pulmonary edema cannot be excluded as a concurrent process. Clinical correlation and comparison with prior imaging recommended.
limitations: Single AP portable view limits assessment; no lateral or upright PA view available. Extensive monitoring equipment (ECG leads, wires, tracheostomy tube) obscures significant portions of lung parenchyma. Supine positioning redistributes pleural fluid posteriorly, making effusion characterization difficult. All analysis agents use the same model (qwen3.6-27b); inter-agent agreement should not be treated as independent cross-model confirmation. DenseNet classifier was trained on PA views; AP portable with device overlay represents out-of-distribution input. PSPNet anatomical segmentation was unreliable on this image, detecting only 3 of 14 structures. No clinical context (vital signs, labs, history) available. Pneumothorax cannot be definitively excluded due to device artifact obscuration of lung apices.

findings: Frontal PA chest radiograph of an adult female patient. Multiple ECG monitoring electrodes and leads are visible overlying the right mid-to-lower lung zone. A central venous catheter enters from the right neck/upper chest region (likely right internal jugular approach) and courses inferiorly along the right mediastinal border, with its tip projecting near the expected SVC-right atrial junction. A radiographic arrow marker is visible in the upper right corner of the image. Lung fields appear clear in visible areas. Cardiac silhouette is within normal limits for size. Mediastinal contours are unremarkable. Trachea is midline. Both costophrenic angles appear sharp. No pneumothorax, pleural effusion, or obvious consolidation identified. Contrast enhancement (CLAHE) of the ECG-covered region and quantitative density comparison of symmetric right and left lung zones do not reveal evidence of underlying parenchymal abnormality.
impression: No acute cardiopulmonary abnormality identified. ECG monitoring equipment and central venous catheter in place. Right mid-to-lower lung zone partially obscured by ECG electrodes; enhancement analysis does not suggest underlying pathology. Clinical correlation recommended regarding the radiographic arrow marker in the upper right corner.
limitations: Single-view study without lateral projection. Pretrained xrv models (DenseNet, ResNet, PSPNet) produced unreliable outputs due to image normalization mismatch (input pixel range [-1024, -526] vs expected [-1024, 1024]). ECG electrodes obscure direct visualization of right mid-to-lower lung parenchyma, though enhancement analysis does not suggest underlying pathology. Radiographic arrow marker in upper right corner is of unknown clinical significance without context. No clinical history available.

findings: AP portable chest radiograph demonstrates bilateral lower zone opacities, more extensive on the left than the right, obscuring both costophrenic angles and hemidiaphragms. Patchy consolidation is present in the right mid-lung zone, with possible air bronchograms. Multiple monitoring devices and tubes are visible throughout the chest, including at least one chest drain on the patient's left side. The cardiac silhouette is difficult to assess due to overlying opacities and AP projection magnification. No definite pneumothorax is identified.
impression: Bilateral lower zone pulmonary opacities with right mid-zone consolidation, in a critically ill patient with multiple monitoring devices. Findings are most consistent with a combination of pleural effusion, dependent atelectasis, and/or consolidation. Clinical correlation is essential.
limitations: Single AP supine view limits assessment; no lateral or upright views available. Multiple monitoring devices obscure lung parenchyma. Limited penetration in lower zones. Pretrained models (xrv DenseNet, PSPNet, ViewModel) trained on adult PA films show reduced reliability for this AP supine image, confirmed by ViewModel's incorrect lateral classification. BiomedCLIP unavailable due to open_clip version incompatibility. Cardiac silhouette assessment unreliable. Bounding boxes are approximate; precise localization requires higher-resolution imaging. All agent analyses use the same underlying model (qwen3.6-27b); agreement between agents does not constitute independent cross-model confirmation.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph shows a moderate-to-large right pleural effusion with meniscus sign, completely obscuring the right costophrenic angle and right hemidiaphragm. Associated right lower lobe compressive atelectasis is likely present but cannot be definitively separated on this single view. The cardiac silhouette appears enlarged (true cardiomegaly vs. AP projection magnification cannot be determined). An implanted venous access port (port-a-cath) is present in the right upper chest wall with catheter coursing toward the SVC. Multiple ECG monitoring electrodes and possible nasogastric tube are visible. The left lung field is relatively clear with a visible gastric bubble beneath the left hemidiaphragm. A white arrow annotation is present on the patient's left side near the clavicle, of unclear significance.
impression: Moderate-to-large right pleural effusion with associated compressive atelectasis in a critically ill patient with multiple indwelling devices. The effusion is the dominant abnormality. Pretrained model scores for effusion were low due to supine positioning and device artifacts; visual assessment takes precedence.
limitations: Single portable AP view without lateral projection limits differentiation of effusion from consolidation and accurate assessment of cardiac size. Supine/semi-erect positioning alters pleural fluid distribution compared to upright studies. Multiple medical devices (port-a-cath, ECG leads) create artifacts that obscure underlying anatomy and confound pretrained model outputs. Image is 1024x1024, potentially downsized from original acquisition. Pretrained model outputs showed significant artifacts: DenseNet121 and ResNet50 gave high Fracture scores (0.52 and 0.87 respectively) likely from device artifacts rather than actual fracture; ViewModel incorrectly classified view as 'Lateral' (0.999). MedSAM segmentation was infeasible on CPU (>900s).

findings: Frontal chest radiograph showing bilateral lower zone linear/plate-like opacities consistent with discoid atelectasis, most prominent in the right lower lung zone. The right lower zone opacity is patchy and somewhat ill-defined, partially silhouetting the right heart border and right hemidiaphragm, suggestive of combined atelectasis and/or consolidation. A well-defined horizontal band-like opacity is present in the left mid-lung zone, characteristic of plate-like atelectasis. Multiple surgical clips are visible in the superior mediastinum/neck region, indicating prior surgical intervention. Cardiac silhouette appears within normal limits. Trachea is midline. No large pleural effusion or pneumothorax identified. Bony structures appear intact.
impression: Bilateral lower zone atelectasis with right basilar opacity (atelectasis vs consolidation). Prior surgical intervention (clips in neck/superior mediastinum). Findings are most consistent with post-operative or post-procedural atelectasis, though superimposed infection (pneumonia) cannot be excluded on a single frontal view.
limitations: Single frontal view without lateral projection limits characterization of anterior/posterior pathology. Lung apices partially excluded due to cropping. DenseNet scores above 0.5 for many categories simultaneously may reflect model uncertainty rather than definitive findings. No prior imaging available for comparison. All analysis agents use the same model (qwen3.6-27b); agreement does not constitute independent cross-model confirmation. MedSAM segmentation failed due to API incompatibility.

findings: Frontal PA chest radiograph of a pediatric/young adolescent patient. There is a subtle, ill-defined area of increased opacity in the right perihilar/mid-to-lower lung zone, independently noted by 4 of 6 council agents on visual inspection. The right and left perihilar ROIs show a minimal intensity difference (mean ~7 units on a 0-255 scale). No overt consolidation, pneumothorax, pleural effusion, cardiomegaly, or bony abnormality is identified. Both costophrenic angles are sharp. The cardiac silhouette is within normal limits. The trachea is midline. Multiple pretrained models classified this as normal or produced unreliable results, likely due to the image being pediatric while models were trained primarily on adult radiographs. The BiomedCLIP model strongly favored 'Normal chest radiograph' (0.993). The DenseNet and ResNet classifiers showed low-confidence, discordant predictions. The ResNetAE autoencoder produced a low-fidelity reconstruction with no focal anomaly signal. MedSAM segmentation captured rib structures rather than the subtle opacity.
impression: Subtle right perihilar/mid-lung opacity of uncertain significance. Given the minimal quantitative difference and the strong 'normal' classification by BiomedCLIP, this may represent normal anatomical overlap of perihilar vascular structures. However, early/patchy pneumonia or atelectasis cannot be excluded without clinical correlation and a lateral view.
limitations: Single-view study without lateral projection limits depth discrimination. Pediatric patient likely falls outside the training distribution of all adult-trained pretrained models (DenseNet, ResNet, PSPNet, ViewModel, ResNetAE), making their outputs unreliable. BiomedCLIP provides only global image-level scoring without spatial localization. MedSAM segmentation was not useful for this low-contrast finding. No clinical history or prior comparison studies available. The subtle nature of the opacity and its indistinct boundaries limit localization precision. CLAHE enhancement was the most useful processing tool, but no analysis method definitively characterized the opacity as pathological versus anatomical.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph. Cardiac silhouette appears borderline prominent, consistent with expected AP projection magnification (10-15%). Both lung fields are clear without focal consolidation, mass, or pneumothorax. No pleural effusion identified; costophrenic angles appear sharp. Mediastinal contours unremarkable, trachea midline. Bony thorax intact without obvious fracture. No medical devices or lines visible. PSPNet segmentation detected 10/14 anatomical structures with high confidence for lungs and heart. DenseNet121 flags Cardiomegaly (0.67), Enlarged Cardiomediastinum (0.62), Pneumonia (0.62); ResNet50 is more conservative with Enlarged Cardiomediastinum (0.62) and Cardiomegaly (0.53) only. Disagreement between classifiers on secondary findings limits their diagnostic utility. CLAHE enhancement revealed no additional focal pathology.
impression: No definite acute cardiopulmonary abnormality identified. Borderline cardiac silhouette cannot be confirmed as true cardiomegaly on AP portable projection. Lungs clear. Limited study by single portable AP view.
limitations: Portable AP projection magnifies cardiac silhouette by 10-15%, preventing definitive assessment of cardiomegaly. Single frontal view only; retrocardiac region partially obscured. 8-bit image with limited dynamic range. No clinical context, comparison studies, or patient demographics available. Automated classifier outputs limited by systematic positive bias (DenseNet) and model disagreement (DenseNet vs ResNet). BiomedCLIP zero-shot analysis unavailable due to offline environment. All 6 agents use the same model family (qwen3.6-27b); agreement does not constitute independent cross-model confirmation. Quantitative CTR estimate (1.67) is a processing artifact from Otsu thresholding and is untrustworthy.

findings: AP portable chest radiograph of a female patient. Severe bilateral degenerative changes of the glenohumeral joints with irregular sclerotic humeral heads, consistent with advanced osteoarthritis or avascular necrosis. Four to five radiopaque surgical clips in the left axillary region, consistent with prior axillary lymph node dissection (likely breast cancer surgery). Apparent cardiomegaly with prominent cardiac silhouette, though assessment limited by AP portable magnification. Bilateral perihilar vascular prominence and mild interstitial markings. Both costophrenic angles appear clear. No focal consolidation, pneumothorax, or large pleural effusion identified. Text labels visible: PORTABLE, AP, L marker.
impression: Severe bilateral glenohumeral joint degenerative disease. Status post left axillary lymph node dissection. Apparent cardiomegaly (AP magnification caveat). Mild pulmonary vascular prominence without definite acute cardiopulmonary process.
limitations: Single AP portable view without lateral comparison. AP projection magnifies cardiac silhouette (typically by >0.15 CTR). DenseNet121 and ResNet50 pathology scores uniformly elevated (0.50-0.68) with limited discriminative value. BiomedCLIP model could not be loaded due to custom architecture incompatibility. Automated surgical clip detection picked up text labels rather than metallic clips. CTR measurement (0.319) unreliable on AP films. Soft tissue overlap from breast shadows partially obscures lung bases.

findings: AP portable chest radiograph of a critically ill ICU patient. Extensive bilateral pulmonary opacities involving all lung zones, significantly more severe on the right. Multiple medical support devices present: endotracheal tube with tip above the carina, right internal jugular central venous catheter, nasogastric/enteral tube, and ECG monitoring leads. Cardiac silhouette appears enlarged with poorly defined borders obscured by adjacent pulmonary opacities. Both costophrenic angles are obscured, consistent with bilateral pleural effusions or basal consolidation. Right hemidiaphragm is completely obscured. Lung windowing and contrast enhancement reveal air bronchograms within the right mid-lung opacity. Quantitative zone analysis confirms right > left opacity burden across all zones (asymmetry ratios 1.18-1.31).
impression: Diffuse bilateral pulmonary opacities, right significantly greater than left, in a critically ill intubated patient. The pattern is most consistent with Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS). Superimposed bilateral severe pneumonia and cardiogenic pulmonary edema cannot be excluded. Bilateral pleural effusions are likely. Apparent cardiomegaly cannot be confirmed due to AP projection and adjacent opacities.
limitations: Single AP portable view without lateral projection. ICU portable technique with suboptimal exposure and magnification. Multiple medical devices (ECG leads, central line, NG tube, ETT) overlap lung fields and may confound automated analysis. PSPNet segmentation failed completely on this image. ResNet-50 pathology scores are near-zero for most labels, suggesting the model is out of distribution for this severely abnormal image. DenseNet Fracture score (0.504) is a likely false positive from medical device artifacts. All analysis agents use the same model (qwen3.6-27b); agreement does not constitute independent cross-model confirmation. Clinical correlation and comparison with prior imaging are essential.

findings: Bilateral lung opacities are present, more prominent in the left lower lung field. There is evidence of pleural effusion on the left. Multiple external monitoring leads and lines are superimposed on the thorax.
impression: Bilateral pulmonary opacities, most likely representing pneumonia or atelectasis with associated pleural effusion, particularly on the left.
limitations: AP projection makes heart size assessment difficult. Presence of external leads and lines partially obscures the lung fields.

Model outputs (DenseNet, PSPNet, BiomedCLIP, MedSAM) were used as cross-checks, not ground truth; PSPNet lung masks had artifacts and BiomedCLIP could not cleanly separate effusion from consolidation. findings: Frontal (AP, likely supine) chest radiograph of a post-sternotomy patient. Median sternotomy with sternal cerclage wires in situ; multiple monitoring leads, ECG electrodes, and a central/mediastinal line are present. There is hazy opacification of the right mid and lower zones, densest medially and at the base, with obscuration of the right hemidiaphragm and partial loss of the right heart border, consistent with pleural effusion/hemothorax and/or basilar atelectasis or consolidation. The right hemithorax is denser than the left in all zones (objective measurement: apex +30, mid +31, base +42), arguing against pneumothorax; no visceral pleural line or hyperlucent hemithorax is seen. The left lung is relatively clear; a small round opacity near the left hilum is most likely a vascular/hilar structure, not a nodule. Cardiac size assessment is limited.
impression: Right mid-to-lower zone opacity (effusion/hemothorax vs basilar atelectasis vs consolidation) in a post-sternotomy patient; no pneumothorax. Sternotomy with cerclage wires and monitoring lines in situ.
limitations: Single frontal (AP, likely supine) view; no lateral view. Bedside/ICU acquisition with motion and slight rotation; low-contrast 8-bit PNG (no raw DICOM HU). Multiple overlying lines, tubes, and ECG electrodes limit assessment. Cardiac size and mediastinal evaluation are limited by the AP projection and the right-sided opacity. Model outputs conflicted (DenseNet vs ResNet); pneumothorax was not visually confirmed and was refuted by the density measurement, so it is excluded.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (L marker, patient's left = image right). A dense, ill-defined, wedge-shaped opacity is present in the left mid-to-lower lung zone, obscuring the medial aspect of the left hemidiaphragm and partially silhouetting the left heart border; the left hemidiaphragm appears relatively elevated/obscured.
