No acute bony abnormality identified. Normal gastric bubble and bowel gas are seen below the left hemidiaphragm.
impression: Left lower lobe opacity, most consistent with atelectasis or consolidation (pneumonia), with a possible small associated left pleural effusion; the right lung is clear.
limitations: Single frontal (PA/AP) projection only — no lateral view to fully distinguish consolidation from atelectasis from effusion, or to assess volume loss. The image is a re-exported/screen-captured PNG with a black detector border and slightly non-uniform brightness, which limits quantitative analysis. The opacity is confluent with the left hemidiaphragm and left heart border (silhouette sign), so its inferior and medial margins are inherently ill-defined and the bounding box necessarily includes the adjacent diaphragm. Model outputs were used only as supportive cross-checks and an anatomical scaffold, not as definitive diagnosis: the pathology classifiers did not strongly activate any single label, and zero-shot/segmentation models carry their own uncertainty. No clinical history is available to correlate.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph of a critically ill patient with a tracheostomy tube, left subclavian central venous catheter, a stent, and multiple ECG leads/cables. Large right pleural effusion: homogeneous opacification of the right mid-to-lower hemithorax with a meniscus-shaped upper border (highest laterally, at the 4th-5th rib level), obscuration of the right hemidiaphragm and right heart border, and contralateral (leftward) tracheal/mediastinal shift. Associated compressive atelectasis of the right lower lobe. The left lung is well-aerated with normal vascular markings; there is a subtle, ill-defined left basilar/retrocardiac opacity (possible small effusion or atelectasis, partly obscured by overlying cables). No definite pneumothorax, no discrete pulmonary nodule or mass, no cardiomegaly, and no pulmonary edema.
impression: Large right pleural effusion with right lower lobe compressive atelectasis, in a critically ill patient with multiple indwelling devices. A possible small left basilar opacity/effusion (uncertain) is also noted.
limitations: Single portable supine/semi-erect AP view; no lateral, upright, or prior comparison view. On a supine film the effusion layers posteriorly, so the meniscus and the fluid volume are only approximate. Multiple overlying devices and cables obscure the left costophrenic angle and lateral chest walls, limiting assessment of the possible small left effusion (recorded as an uncertain observation). The whole-image classifier (DenseNet) gave non-specific scores; segmentation masks can leak at opacity borders. The etiology of the effusion (transudate vs exudate, hemothorax vs empyema) cannot be determined from the radiograph alone.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph demonstrating a diffuse bilateral multifocal nodular pattern: numerous discrete, round-to-oval pulmonary nodules/opacities scattered throughout both lung fields, approximately 3-10 mm in size (largest ~10-12 mm in the left mid-lung), present in the upper, mid and lower zones of both lungs. The cardiomediastinal silhouette appears within normal limits; no definite large pleural effusion, pneumothorax, or focal lobar consolidation is seen, and no displaced rib fracture is identified.
impression: Diffuse bilateral multifocal pulmonary nodules. The size range (~3-10 mm) and random bilateral distribution favor a hematogenous or granulomatous process; the leading considerations are pulmonary metastases, a miliary/granulomatous infection (e.g. miliary tuberculosis or miliary fungal), or sarcoidosis. CT chest and clinical correlation are recommended to characterize the nodules.
limitations: Single frontal projection only (no lateral view and no prior study for comparison); 2D projection with overlapping structures and reduced contrast/haziness. Bounding boxes were derived from visual inspection cross-checked against automated blob detection and 3x-magnified crops; the smallest nodules (~3 mm) can overlap normal pulmonary vessels, so a few borderline sub-centimeter opacities were described but not individually boxed. Image-level AI pathology classifiers behaved noisily on this film (e.g. spurious Fracture/Pneumothorax activation) and were used only as weak corroboration, not to support any specific finding. The exact etiology (metastatic vs infectious vs granulomatous) cannot be determined from a single radiograph.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph of a critically ill patient with a midline tracheostomy tube, a left subclavian large-bore central venous catheter, a right-sided chest drain, and ECG electrodes/leads in situ. There is a dense, near-whiteout airspace opacity of the right upper and mid zones abutting the mediastinum. Patchy, ill-defined airspace opacities are present in the right lower zone and diffusely throughout the left lung (upper, mid and lower zones). The trachea is midline with no gross mediastinal shift. No pneumothorax is identified and no large pleural effusion is seen. The cardiac silhouette is partly obscured by adjacent opacities; no gross cardiomegaly is appreciable on this AP view. No acute rib fracture is identified.
impression: Dense right upper/mid-zone consolidation (most likely pneumonia) with multifocal bilateral airspace disease in a tracheostomized, centrally line-accessed ICU patient with a right chest drain in situ. No pneumothorax or large effusion.
limitations: Single portable AP view; no lateral or prior comparison films. AP projection causes magnification and reduced detail, and inspiration is suboptimal. Overlying devices (tracheostomy tube, central line, chest drain, ECG leads) and the patient's adducted right arm overlap the right hemithorax, limiting assessment of the lateral right lung and mimicking/obscuring pathology. Whole-image classifier (DenseNet) and zero-shot (BiomedCLIP) scores are uncalibrated in this covariate-shifted setting and were used only as supportive cross-checks. The dense opacity is a gradient, so the box captures the consolidated core; its faint periphery and the blend into the patchy right lower zone are not sharply defined. Air bronchograms were not definitively resolved, so consolidation cannot be fully separated from a collapse/effusion component.

findings: AP portable chest radiograph. Bilateral patchy, confluent airspace opacities with mid-lower zone predominance (right more confluent than left), including a denser rounded confluent component in the right mid-lung. Enlarged, hazy cardiac silhouette. Probable small bilateral pleural effusions (blunted costophrenic angles). Upper lung zones relatively aerated. Right-sided dual-lumen central venous catheter in situ. No definite pneumothorax. A drawn arrow at the extreme left lateral chest wall does not correspond to a clear focal pulmonary lesion (likely skin fold/external annotation).
impression: Bilateral multifocal mid-lower lung opacities in a patient with a central venous catheter, most consistent with multifocal pneumonia or pulmonary edema. The patchy/confluent pattern and relatively low edema scores favor pneumonia, while the enlarged cardiac silhouette and probable effusions keep cardiogenic edema in the differential. Clinical correlation (labs, BNP/procalcitonin, history) and comparison with prior imaging are recommended.
limitations: Single AP portable (bedside) projection magnifies the cardiac silhouette and reduces detail, so true cardiomegaly and subtle findings are hard to quantify; no lateral view or prior images for comparison. Image is an 8-bit PNG (quantized, not 16-bit DICOM), limiting subtle density discrimination. Hazy, ill-defined opacity margins make exact bounding-box extents approximate. Whole-image pretrained classifiers (DenseNet/ResNet) disagree on mass/nodule, so no discrete neoplasm was claimed; they inform but do not localize. Clinical data (labs, history) are unavailable, so pneumonia vs edema cannot be definitively distinguished.

findings: Portable AP supine chest radiograph of an intubated, centrally accessed patient. Bilateral diffuse patchy and confluent airspace opacities, most prominent in the mid and lower lung zones with relative sparing of the apices: the right mid-lower zone shows confluent patchy opacification and the left mid-lower zone shows hazy confluent opacification that partially obscures the left heart border. The cardiac silhouette appears enlarged (possible cardiomegaly). The costophrenic angles are blunted/obscured bilaterally, consistent with possible small pleural effusions or dependent atelectasis. In-situ devices: an endotracheal tube with its tip at/above the carina (appropriate position), a left subclavian/neck central venous catheter terminating near the SVC, and overlying external ECG electrodes and lead wires. No pneumothorax is identified and no acute rib fracture is seen.
impression: Bilateral diffuse airspace opacities (infiltrates), mid- and lower-zone predominant with relative apical sparing. The pattern is most consistent with pulmonary edema (cardiogenic and/or non-cardiogenic) or multifocal/bilateral pneumonia; ARDS/aspiration are also in the differential. Possible cardiomegaly and possible small bilateral pleural effusions. In an intubated, centrally accessed patient this most likely represents a diffuse alveolar process; clinical correlation is required.
limitations: Single portable AP supine view with no PA or lateral comparison: the heart is magnified, pneumothorax and effusions are harder to detect (fluid layers posteriorly when supine), and rotation/positioning may affect appearance. Overlying external hardware (ECG electrodes, lead wires, and lines) obscures parts of the lungs and mediastinum. Pretrained models (DenseNet121, ResNet50, PSPNet, BiomedCLIP) were trained mainly on frontal chest radiographs; this AP supine portable film with overlying hardware is partly off-distribution - the PSPNet lung masks over-included chest wall (making the CTR and the initial automated dense-boxes unreliable; these were discarded) and the classifiers do not localize. The etiology of the diffuse opacities (edema vs pneumonia vs ARDS vs aspiration) cannot be definitively distinguished on a single film; there is no prior imaging for comparison; clinical correlation is required.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph of a monitored/ICU patient (multiple ECG leads and external monitoring hardware overlying the chest; a radiolucent line descends from the neck in the right paratracheal region). There are bilateral hazy, patchy opacities in the lower lung zones, more prominent on the right, with a reticular/subsegmental pattern above the hemidiaphragms, consistent with atelectasis. Lung volumes are low and the right hemidiaphragm sits at a normal-to-mildly-high position (only slightly higher than the left, within normal variance). No pneumothorax is seen (lung markings reach the periphery at both apices). There is no definite pleural effusion and no cardiomegaly or widened mediastinum on this AP projection. The small round density in the left upper abdomen is a non-metallic gastric button/fold, not a foreign body.
impression: Bilateral basal (lower lobe) atelectasis in a monitored patient with low lung volumes; early/patchy pneumonia cannot be excluded. No pneumothorax, no definite effusion, and no cardiomegaly.
limitations: Single portable AP (supine/semi-upright ICU) projection without a lateral view or prior comparison; low lung volumes and overlying monitoring hardware/lines limit assessment. Atelectasis versus early consolidation and a small pleural effusion cannot be definitively distinguished on one AP film. Pretrained-model outputs (DenseNet pathology scores, PSPNet segmentation) were used only as corroborative/soft evidence: the classifier scores hovered near the operating threshold and the segmentation masks leaked across the lateral chest wall, so neither was relied on to establish a finding. All focal findings were confirmed by direct visual inspection of the original and enhanced images.

findings: Frontal (AP/PA) chest radiograph extending into the upper abdomen. The dominant abnormality is in the abdomen: (1) a markedly distended, gas-filled viscus in the left upper quadrant with a single horizontal air-fluid level (gas dome over a flat fluid line), located below the left hemidiaphragm; (2) multiple gas-filled, prominent/dilated bowel loops in the upper and mid abdomen. No definite focal pulmonary consolidation, no definite pleural effusion, and no pneumothorax. Mild linear/patchy density at the right base (likely atelectasis). No free subdiaphragmatic air identified. The cardiac silhouette appears widened (AP magnification, not reliably assessable). Multiple devices/artifacts are present: a tracheostomy tube in the cervical trachea, a long catheter coursing through the right hemithorax, and external objects (a round metallic button over the right mid-lung, a battery pack over the left shoulder, and a safety pin over the left axilla).
impression: Markedly gas-distended upper abdomen — a large distended gas-filled viscus in the left upper quadrant with an air-fluid level plus multiple gas-filled bowel loops — most consistent with bowel/gastric distension (obstruction or ileus). No definite acute focal pulmonary pathology.
limitations: Single frontal view; AP vs PA not definitively labeled and no lateral view, so the stomach vs colonic identity of the viscus cannot be confirmed, bowel dilation cannot be quantified, and the apparently widened cardiac silhouette is likely AP magnification. Supine positioning limits detection of free air and small effusions; no definite free subdiaphragmatic air was seen but a small amount cannot be fully excluded without upright/lateral-decubitus views. Multiple devices and external artifacts (tracheostomy, catheter, button, battery pack, safety pin) overlap the lung fields and may mask subtle findings. Pretrained chest-pathology models (DenseNet) gave no confident focal chest pathology and do not assess the abdomen; the wrist-fracture YOLO detector was out-of-domain and was not used for any finding. No clinical context is available.

findings: Frontal (AP/supine) chest radiograph of a young child. The lungs are clear with normal vascular markings; no focal consolidation, mass, effusion, or pneumothorax is identified. The cardiac silhouette is enlarged but within the expected range for age and AP projection. Three radiopaque findings are present: (1) a complex metallic-density object (a bar with an upward arrow-like tip, a crossbar, a ring, and a thin tubing loop) projecting over the patient's left shoulder/deltoid, superficial to the clavicle, and clipped at the right edge of the image; (2) a thin, smooth, radiopaque tube/line coursing obliquely from the patient's right axilla to the left lower abdomen; and (3) a small bony-density angular structure near the right upper mediastinum (likely a rib end, of uncertain significance). A large gastric air bubble is present under the left hemidiaphragm. A black bar runs along the left edge of the image and the bottom is cropped.
impression: Pediatric chest radiograph with no acute cardiopulmonary disease. The salient findings are radiopaque foreign bodies/devices: a metallic object over the left shoulder and an oblique tube/line crossing the chest (most consistent with an external catheter/feeding tube or artifact); their nature and position require clinical correlation.
limitations: 8-bit pre-windowed PNG (not raw DICOM) with limited dynamic range. Supine AP projection with a magnified cardiac silhouette. A large gastric air bubble obscures the left lower zone. A black bar along the left edge and cropping at the bottom exclude part of the anatomy. The nature of the radiopaque objects (external artifact vs indwelling device vs foreign body) cannot be determined without clinical history, a lateral view, or correlation. CXR AI classifiers (DenseNet121, BiomedCLIP) flagged 'opacity/consolidation', but no focal consolidation was confirmed (diffuse Grad-CAM, ResNet50 negative, anatomical segmenters showing uniform lungs, and clear lung windows) - likely an out-of-distribution response to the large pediatric heart/mediastinum and 8-bit haze. The small right paratracheal object is likely a rib end and was not localised as a lesion.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (pediatric, PA/AP). A hazy, ill-defined opacity in the left lower zone (retrocardiac) obscures the left hemidiaphragm (silhouette sign), while the lateral left costophrenic sulcus remains aerated/preserved. The right lung is clear with a sharp right hemidiaphragm. The cardiothoracic ratio is normal (measured ~0.33), so there is no cardiomegaly. A thin curvilinear line in the right mid-lower lung is consistent with an azygos fissure (normal anatomic variant). Mild S-shaped thoracolumbar scoliosis is present. No pneumothorax, no large pleural effusion, and no rib fracture is seen.
impression: Left lower zone (retrocardiac) pulmonary opacity, most consistent with left lower lobe atelectasis or pneumonia. No cardiomegaly. Incidental azygos fissure (normal variant) and mild scoliosis.
limitations: Single frontal projection with no lateral view, so lingular vs lower-lobe location cannot be separated and a small effusion cannot be quantified. The pediatric AP projection (magnification) and the retrocardiac location limit assessment of the opacity's exact extent, and its margins are hazy/ill-defined. Pretrained models behaved out-of-domain on this pediatric chest film: DenseNet pathology scores were indeterminate (many mutually-exclusive labels at ~0.5) and were not relied upon; the YOLOv8 wrist detector was out of domain (it detected only the 'L' side marker); and PSPNet/MedSAM were used only after visual validation of their masks, as anatomical/geometric corroboration rather than primary evidence. The etiology (atelectasis vs pneumonia) cannot be determined from a single frontal view without clinical correlation.

findings: AP (portable, likely supine) chest radiograph of a critically ill, intubated patient. Diffuse bilateral airspace opacities with a patchy/mottled distribution, most confluent in the mid-to-lower zones and perihilarly; the upper zones are relatively better aerated (a gravity-dependent gradient is present). The hemidiaphragms and costophrenic angles are obscured by the lower-zone opacification, with probable bilateral pleural effusion contributing. The cardiac silhouette and mediastinum are partially obscured; the cardiomediastinal contour appears widened (likely exaggerated by the AP/supine projection). A midline endotracheal/tracheal tube is present in the trachea (tip not sharply assessable on this single view). A coiled thin radiopaque catheter/tube projects over the left mid-chest, most consistent with an external coiled line on the chest wall. Bilateral ECG electrode snaps and multiple external monitoring cables are present; a thin linear radiopacity crosses the neck (probable external cable, uncertain significance). No definite pneumothorax. No discrete focal pulmonary mass or nodule is identified (the abnormality is patchy/diffuse, not a focal lesion).
impression: Diffuse bilateral airspace opacities (airspace disease) in an intubated/critically ill patient, most pronounced in the mid-lower zones and perihilarly, most consistent with multifocal pneumonia or pulmonary edema/ARDS; probable bilateral pleural effusions. A coiled external catheter/tube overlies the left mid-chest. No focal mass, nodule, or pneumothorax.
limitations: Single AP (portable, likely supine) projection with no lateral view; AP/supine technique exaggerates cardiomediastinal width and diaphragmatic elevation. Low overall contrast/underexposure and body habitus obscure the hemidiaphragms, costophrenic angles and heart borders, limiting assessment of effusion volume and cardiac size. Multiple overlying devices (airway tube, ECG snaps, coiled catheter, external monitoring cables) clutter the field and some linear opacities are of uncertain significance (external vs internal). A single static image cannot definitively distinguish pulmonary edema/ARDS from multifocal pneumonia; clinical correlation and serial imaging are recommended. Model outputs (view classifier, DenseNet/ResNet pathology scores, BiomedCLIP zero-shot) were used only as supportive second opinions; the UNet fine-grained anatomical segmentation was unreliable on this image and was not used to support any finding. Bounding boxes for the diffuse opacities are approximate, as the process is diffuse and extends beyond the boxed mid-lower zones into the more mildly affected upper zones.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph of an adult female (bilateral breast soft-tissue shadows) with low lung volumes (elevated hemidiaphragms). An implanted venous access port is present in the left upper chest (left infraclavicular region); the reservoir is in the expected position and the catheter courses cephalad and then medially toward the superior vena cava. There is a hazy, ill-defined increased density in the left mid-to-lower lung zone (retrocardiac/paracardiac) that partially obscures the left hemidiaphragm and is more opaque than the corresponding right region. The right lung is clear with a sharp right costophrenic angle. The cardiac silhouette is normal in size and the mediastinum is not widened. No pneumothorax or pleural effusion is identified.
impression: Chest X-ray in a patient with an implanted port. The principal abnormality is a subtle left lower-zone opacity, most consistent with atelectasis in the setting of low lung volumes, with early consolidation a consideration. No pneumothorax, no effusion, normal cardiac size.
limitations: Single frontal view (no lateral). The image is an 8-bit display-processed PNG (not raw DICOM) with a compressed dynamic range, limiting subtle density assessment. Bilateral breast shadows superimpose over both lower lung zones and the implanted device overlies the left lung, both confounding the left lower zone. The left opacity is hazy and ill-defined, so distinguishing atelectasis, early consolidation, and technical factors (low lung volumes + breast shadow) is uncertain. The catheter tip position could not be precisely assessed on a single frontal view. The pathology classifiers and segmentation models were trained on raw DICOM and applied here to a processed image, so their outputs are supportive rather than definitive; BiomedCLIP zero-shot was uninformative on this low-contrast image.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. Markedly elevated left hemidiaphragm, with its dome ~73-78 px (about 2-3 intercostal spaces) above the right hemidiaphragm, and a gastric bubble lying directly beneath the elevated left dome. Increased hazy opacity in the left lower/mid lung zone above the elevated diaphragm (ROI mean intensity 111.6 vs 67.7 at the comparable right position, diff +44), consistent with compressive/segmental atelectasis. Indwelling right pigtail pleural catheter with a coiled tip in the right upper zone and the shaft descending along the right mediastinal border toward the right lower zone. Left infraclavicular/pectoral implantable venous port with its catheter coursing inferiorly and medially toward the SVC. Two small, dense, oval metallic densities overlying the left lateral 2nd-3rd ribs (indeterminate: surgical clips / metallic foreign bodies / external). External ECG monitoring electrode over the right mid lung. Right lung well aerated with a sharp right costophrenic angle; no pneumothorax identified.
impression: Markedly elevated left hemidiaphragm with associated left lower lobe atelectasis/opacity; indwelling right pleural pigtail catheter and left chest port in situ.
limitations: Single frontal projection only (no lateral), limiting anterior-posterior discrimination and the distinction between true diaphragmatic elevation and a subpulmonic effusion. Indwelling devices (pigtail, port) and an external ECG electrode overlap and partially obscure the underlying anatomy. Image supplied as a processed 8-bit PNG (no original DICOM/Hounsfield units), limiting precise quantification. Pathology classifiers (ResNet50-512-all, DenseNet121-224-all) returned only weak, non-specific borderline scores and are image-level (non-localizing) second-opinion screens only. The left chest-wall metallic densities are of uncertain nature (internal vs external).

findings: Frontal chest radiograph of a monitored patient with a right-sided chest tube, a right central venous catheter, and multiple ECG/monitoring electrodes. There is a patchy, heterogeneous airspace opacity in the right mid-to-lower lung zone with preserved lung markings and interspersed air spaces, causing a silhouette sign at the right heart border. The left lung is clear. There is no definite pneumothorax (right apex is aerated with no visible visceral pleural line) and no free subdiaphragmatic air (pneumoperitoneum). No definite cardiomegaly or pulmonary edema.
impression: Right mid-lower zone airspace opacity with a consolidation/atelectasis pattern, most consistent with right middle lobe / right lower lobe consolidation (pneumonia) with associated atelectasis, in a monitored patient with a right chest tube in situ.
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral view). Multiple overlying monitoring devices and tubes (ECG snaps, chest tube, central venous catheter) partially obscure lung markings. The opacity abuts the diaphragm and heart, so its inferior and medial margins are approximate. A single frontal film cannot fully distinguish consolidation from atelectasis or from a partially drained effusion. Pretrained model outputs (DenseNet, BiomedCLIP) are whole-image, non-localizing, and only partly in-distribution for this device-laden ICU film, so they were used only as supporting opinions, not to establish findings or the box.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. A small, well-circumscribed round opacity of approximately 10 mm is present in the left mid lung zone, most consistent with a small pulmonary nodule (a normal end-on pulmonary vessel cannot be excluded on a single frontal view). A rounded density in the right hilum / right mid zone is most consistent with the normal end-on right interlobar pulmonary artery. The cardiac silhouette is normal in size (cardiothoracic ratio approximately 0.39). No pleural effusion, pneumothorax, focal consolidation, or pulmonary edema. The trachea is midline, the mediastinum is of normal width, and the visualized osseous structures are intact.
impression: Small rounded opacity in the left mid lung zone, most consistent with a solitary pulmonary nodule; comparison with prior imaging and/or CT is suggested for further characterization.
limitations: Single frontal (PA/AP) projection only; no lateral view and no prior images for comparison, so the depth of the left mid-zone opacity cannot be assessed and an end-on pulmonary vessel cannot be excluded. The right hilar rounded density was judged a normal vascular structure on the basis of its low relative density, which cannot be fully confirmed on one view. Pretrained classifier outputs (DenseNet/ResNet/BiomedCLIP) are whole-image second opinions without localization and showed weak/inconsistent nodule support. Lesion localization is in pixels of a 1024x1024 image; physical size (~10 mm) is an estimate from assumed field of view.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph, well penetrated and adequately inspired. The lungs are clear and well-aerated bilaterally, with no definite focal consolidation, pulmonary nodule, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax; both costophrenic angles are sharp. The cardiomediastinal silhouette and hila are within normal limits, and the trachea is midline. The visualised osseous structures (ribs, clavicles, scapulae, spine) are intact. A subtle hazy appearance in the mid-lateral right upper zone corresponds to normal pulmonary vascular markings: objective pixel-intensity analysis shows that this region is not denser than the adjacent or contralateral lung (it is in fact the most aerated part of the right upper zone), so it is not a true focal opacity. A small, indeterminate dense focus is present at the left heart border (approx x=672, y=703), which is most likely a small vessel-on-end or a tiny calcification and is not clearly projecting within aerated lung.
impression: No definite acute cardiopulmonary abnormality and no confident focal pulmonary lesion. The only notable finding is a small, indeterminate dense focus at the left heart border (likely a vessel-on-end or a tiny incidental calcification).
limitations: Single frontal projection only (no lateral view), which limits assessment of subtle focal findings and the exact plane/localisation of the small left heart-border focus. That focus is indeterminate in nature (vessel-on-end vs tiny calcification vs cardiac/mediastinal structure) and is not clearly intrapulmonary. The image is 8-bit with moderate contrast, making subtle parenchymal findings difficult to assess. The perceived right-upper-zone 'haziness' was objectively shown to be normal pulmonary vasculature rather than a true opacity. No clinical history was available to correlate with the findings.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. A bright, metallic, clip-shaped external artifact projects over the patient's left shoulder / medial clavicle, partly outside the body silhouette (top-right of image). The lung fields are otherwise well aerated; there is a subtle area of fine reticular/interstitial markings in the medial left lower lung zone adjacent to the heart border (nonspecific). The cardiac silhouette and mediastinum are normal in size and contour, the trachea is midline, both costophrenic angles are sharp, and there is no focal consolidation, mass, pneumothorax, or pleural effusion. A normal gastric air bubble is present beneath the left hemidiaphragm.
impression: Near-normal frontal chest radiograph. The only definite focal abnormality is an external metallic (clip-like) artifact over the left shoulder; there is additionally a subtle, nonspecific reticular change in the left lower lung zone (mild atelectasis vs early infiltrate vs normal variant). No definite acute cardiopulmonary abnormality.
limitations: Single frontal projection only (no lateral view), which limits depth/localization of the subtle left-lower opacity. The metallic object is an external artifact (likely a clothing/lead clip); its exact identity cannot be determined from the image alone. The left-lower-zone reticular change is subtle and at the threshold of detectability and may be a normal variant. Pretrained pathology models (DenseNet-121, ResNet-50) returned only weak/borderline scores (no confident pathology), and BiomedCLIP zero-shot ranked the chest as normal; whole-image models cannot localize small focal objects, so the small peripheral clip is not reliably 'seen' by them. Interpretation should be correlated clinically and with additional views if warranted.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (orientation confirmed by the 'L' marker; AI view classifier also reads Frontal). Large hazy opacity of the left mid-to-lower hemithorax with a concave (meniscus) superior border that obscures the left hemidiaphragm, the left costophrenic angle and part of the left heart border, consistent with a moderate-to-large left pleural effusion with adjacent atelectasis. The right lung is clear with a sharp right costophrenic angle and no pneumothorax. Multiple metallic screws of orthopedic fixation are present in the right shoulder / clavicle-coracoid region (post-surgical). One or more radiopaque catheter(s)/line(s) traverse the left hemithorax and upper mediastinum, including a coiled/kinked segment over the lower thoracic spine (T12-L1) and a thin circular loop over the left mid-zone; their identity (central line, chest drain, or external lead) cannot be determined from a single frontal view. A gastric air bubble is seen below the left hemidiaphragm.
impression: Moderate-to-large left pleural effusion (with adjacent atelectasis/consolidation) in a patient with post-surgical right-shoulder hardware and an indwelling catheter/line. No pneumothorax; right lung clear.
limitations: Single frontal projection (no lateral view), so effusion volume and posterior layering cannot be fully assessed and a small pneumothorax or posterior effusion could be under-appreciated. The image has quantum noise and slight rotation. The patient has orthopedic hardware and indwelling catheter(s)/lines, which are out-of-distribution for the AI pathology classifiers (DenseNet/ResNet); those produced atypical, low-confidence and mutually inconsistent outputs and were therefore NOT used to support any finding (retained only as a documented weak cross-check; the ResNet 'Mass' 0.94 is judged a false positive). The coiled catheter's identity, and the exact medial extent of the effusion (which abuts the obscured heart border), are uncertain. findings: Frontal chest radiograph. The right hemithorax is markedly abnormal: a large heterogeneous opacity involves the right upper, mid and lower zones. There is a rounded soft-tissue mass with a central lucent area in the medial right mid zone adjacent to the hilum. The right upper zone shows opacification with a horizontal band of the elevated minor (horizontal) fissure and retraction of the upper lobe toward the hilum (right upper lobe collapse pattern). The right lower zone shows a patchy reticular and dense opacity with an elevated right hemidiaphragm and an obscured right costophrenic angle (consolidation and/or pleural effusion). The trachea and mediastinum are subtly shifted toward the right (toward the opacity side), consistent with a mild volume-loss component. The left lung is well aerated except for a small, well-defined rounded density in the left mid zone. No definite pneumothorax. No displaced rib fracture identified.
impression: Large right-sided pulmonary mass with right upper lobe collapse and right basal consolidation/effusion, most consistent with a right lung neoplasm (e.g. carcinoma) with post-obstructive change; additionally a small indeterminate left mid-zone pulmonary nodule.
limitations: Single frontal projection only (no lateral view for 3D localization); 8-bit PNG without DICOM metadata (exposure, patient info). Superimposition of ribs, spine and mediastinum partly obscures the right hilum, limiting precise mass margin definition. The mediastinal/tracheal shift is subtle and partly confounded by patient rotation. The left mid-zone density is small and may be a vessel end or rib cross-section rather than a true nodule. Pretrained model outputs (pathology classifier, structure segmentation, zero-shot vision-language, prompted segmentation) were used only to corroborate directly visible findings after sanity checks; none was allowed to create a finding, and a model-suggested pneumothorax was rejected as not visually confirmed.

findings: Frontal (PA/AP) chest radiograph. The left lung is clear; the left lower-zone opacity is the left heart border (silhouette sign), not lung parenchyma. No pleural effusion, no pneumothorax, and no other focal parenchymal lesion is identified.
impression: Focal hazy opacity in the right mid lung zone, most consistent with a pulmonary nodule or mass or a focal consolidation, together with borderline cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio ~0.53). The opacity is ill-defined and overlies the rib/chest wall, so its exact nature and margins are uncertain on this single frontal film.
limitations: Single frontal (PA/AP) projection with no lateral view, so the depth and true shape of the opacity cannot be established. The opacity is hazy and ill-defined and overlies the rib/lateral chest wall, so the bounding box is approximate. The cardiac silhouette is borderline enlarged (cardiothoracic ratio ~0.53); this is a non-focal finding and is not localized as a lesion. Whole-image pathology classifiers are non-localizing and were used only as support; zero-shot BiomedCLIP and the autoencoder residual were sanity/support checks only. findings: AP portable chest radiograph. Patchy airspace and interstitial (reticular-nodular) opacity in the right lung, most prominent in the mid and lower zones, with relative sparing of the left lung. A dual-lumen central venous catheter (likely hemodialysis catheter) is present, entering from the right neck/supraclavicular region and descending through the right paratracheal/mediastinal region, with its tip in the region of the superior vena cava/upper right atrium (appropriate position). The cardiac silhouette appears prominent, but the measured cardiothoracic ratio is normal (~0.43), consistent with AP magnification and low lung volumes rather than true cardiomegaly. No pneumothorax, no large pleural effusion, and no displaced rib fracture identified on careful review. The right costophrenic angle is somewhat hazy, and a small effusion cannot be entirely excluded.
impression: Patchy right-lung airspace/interstitial opacity, most consistent with pneumonia/infiltrate. A dual-lumen central venous catheter is in situ and appropriately positioned with its tip in the SVC/RA. No significant cardiomegaly, no large effusion, no pneumothorax, and no rib fracture.
limitations: Single AP portable view (no lateral). AP projection magnifies the cardiac silhouette and overlying soft tissue/upper abdominal contents obscure the lung bases, limiting base assessment. Findings were corroborated by multiple pretrained models (DenseNet, BiomedCLIP, PSPNet), but these are population-level, cannot localize, and can be wrong on individual images. MedSAM did not delineate a discrete mass (consistent with a patchy process). A community bone-fracture classifier reported 'Fractured 0.91', which was rejected after careful visual rib review showed no fracture (likely confounded by the radiopaque catheter / out-of-domain). The exact etiology of the opacity (infection vs atelectasis vs edema) cannot be definitively distinguished on a single radiograph.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. A large homogeneous opacity occupies the right lower and mid hemithorax, with a concave upper border (meniscus) rising to approximately mid-thorax along the lateral chest wall; it obscures the right hemidiaphragm and the right heart border (silhouette sign), consistent with a moderate-to-large right pleural effusion. An adjacent hazy reticular opacity (atelectasis) is present in the right paracardiac/lower zone. The left lung is clear, without focal consolidation, effusion, or pneumothorax. A central venous catheter is present, entering from the left subclavian/brachiocephalic region, crossing the midline, and descending in the superior vena cava. The trachea is midline. A thin external monitoring lead crosses the left lateral chest wall. No rib fracture identified.
impression: Moderate-to-large right pleural effusion with adjacent right lower lobe atelectasis. A left-sided central venous catheter is in the superior vena cava (tip not clearly visualized due to upper-mediastinal overpenetration).
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral), so effusion vs consolidation and free vs loculated fluid cannot be fully separated. Upper-mediastinal overpenetration obscures the CVC tip, so its exact tip position cannot be confirmed (course is consistent with the SVC). Cardiac size assessment is limited by the effusion obscuring the right heart border. The image is a resampled 8-bit PNG without DICOM metadata (unknown original windowing). The effusion bounding box necessarily includes adjacent atelectatic lung and the obscured right heart border, plus a thin band of aerated lung at its upper-left corner. Model outputs (DenseNet, PSPNet) are approximate and were used only as corroborating evidence, not as the sole basis for any finding.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (L marker top-right). The cardiac silhouette is prominent/enlarged, with the left heart border extending laterally into the left hemithorax (cardiothoracic ratio ~0.49 by manual landmark measurement and up to ~0.56 by segmentation). A thin linear (subsegmental) atelectatic band is present in the left lower lung field, just above the left hemidiaphragm. There is a faint, ill-defined opacity in the right mid lung zone (most likely an end-on pulmonary vessel; a nodule was not confirmed on high-magnification and intensity analysis). No pneumothorax, no large pleural effusion, no lobar consolidation, no discrete mediastinal mass, and no rib fracture. The lungs are otherwise well-aerated and the costophrenic angles are essentially sharp.
impression: Borderline/mild cardiomegaly (prominent cardiac-mediastinal silhouette) with linear left basilar atelectasis; no acute focal pulmonary process. The prominent heart is the dominant finding.
limitations: Single frontal projection with no confirmation of PA vs AP (an AP film overestimates heart size, so the cardiomegaly is only borderline); no lateral view; no clinical metadata (PNG only). Heart size was judged from manual CTR and segmentation rather than the DenseNet classifier, whose cardiomegaly score was left-right flip-unstable. The faint right mid-zone opacity is not a confirmed nodule (no discrete intensity peak; classifier/zero-shot scores neutral), so it is not localized as a lesion. Pretrained models were run on the full image resized to 224/512 rather than a training-style center crop, which may reduce sensitivity for peripheral findings. Bounding boxes are approximate.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. A focal, rounded, somewhat ill-defined pulmonary opacity is present in the right mid-to-lower lung zone (paracardiac), measuring approximately 101 x 86 pixels. A vague area of increased opacity is also noted in the left lower lung zone adjacent to the left heart border (uncertain; may overlap the heart border or vessels). The cardiomediastinal silhouette is normal in size (cardiothoracic ratio ~0.35). There is no significant hemidiaphragm elevation (the right dome is slightly higher than the left, within normal limits). No pleural effusion, no pneumothorax, and no definite rib or other bony fracture is identified. Mild bibasilar reticular markings are present.
impression: Focal rounded pulmonary opacity in the right mid-to-lower lung zone (paracardiac) - differential includes a pulmonary nodule/mass, focal atelectasis, or early consolidation. No other acute cardiopulmonary abnormality.
limitations: Single frontal projection; no lateral view to confirm the 3D position of the opacity or exclude a vessel running anteroposteriorly. The opacity is subtle in density (~+13 gray levels vs adjacent lung), limiting specificity. The image is an 8-bit PNG (compressed), limiting subtle density assessment. No prior imaging for comparison (growth/stability cannot be assessed). Patient age/sex/clinical context unknown. Model outputs (DenseNet, BiomedCLIP, MedSAM, PSPNet) are supportive but not definitive; PSPNet was unreliable for fine localization (used only for diaphragm/heart measurements); the YOLO wrist detector and the community fracture classifier were out-of-domain (the fracture classifier's 'Fractured 0.89' was a false positive - bones are intact on bone-window views). A vascular confluence cannot be excluded with certainty from a single frontal view.

findings: Frontal (AP) chest radiograph. Diffuse bilateral pulmonary opacities with a reticular/ground-glass (interstitial) and airspace pattern, most prominent in the mid-to-lower lung zones and slightly more extensive/opacified in the right lung than the left. Both costophrenic angles appear blunted/obscured. The cardiac silhouette appears prominent, partly due to the AP projection. Multiple ECG monitoring leads and an external radiopaque disc/marker overlie the image. No pneumothorax, no focal lobar consolidation with air bronchograms, no discrete mass, and no definite rib fracture are identified.
impression: Diffuse bilateral pulmonary opacities (interstitial/ground-glass with a dependent/basal component), most consistent with a diffuse infiltrative process such as atypical or viral pneumonia; pulmonary edema and other diffuse airspace disease remain in the differential.
limitations: Single portable AP projection (no PA or lateral view), which magnifies the cardiac silhouette and limits assessment of cardiomegaly (the mask-based cardiothoracic ratio of 0.586 conflicts with the classifier's low cardiomegaly score, so it is not called as a definite finding). Overlying ECG leads and an external radiopaque marker can mimic or obscure pathology. The opacity is diffuse with ill-defined margins, so the bounding boxes approximate the extent of the abnormally opacified parenchyma rather than a sharply circumscribed lesion. Pretrained models (DenseNet, UNet) were used as corroborating evidence, not ground truth; the wrist-fracture YOLO detector was out of domain and treated as a negative. No prior images for comparison and no clinical context (symptoms, labs, ABG) were available.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph. Dense, confluent opacity in the left lower lung zone that silhouettes and obscures the left hemidiaphragm and the left heart border, consistent with a left lower lobe process (consolidation/collapse, possible pleural effusion component). Diffuse patchy airspace and interstitial opacities throughout the mid and lower zones of both lungs, more confluent at the left base. Right internal jugular central venous catheter in situ with the tip at the superior vena cava / cavo-atrial junction. Multiple external monitoring artifacts (ECG electrode snaps and a lead wire) and external orthopedic splints with metallic components overlying both upper arms/shoulders. No definite pneumothorax in the visualized apices. The cardiac silhouette appears widened, exaggerated by the AP projection.
impression: Bilateral pulmonary airspace disease (pulmonary edema/ARDS versus multifocal pneumonia) with a dominant dense left lower lobe opacity (consolidation/collapse, possible effusion), in a critically ill patient with a right internal jugular central line and external monitoring/splinting artifacts.
limitations: Single portable AP view (no lateral), with AP magnification exaggerating the cardiac silhouette and reducing basilar detail. Overlying external hardware (orthopedic splints, ECG electrodes/leads) obscures parts of the lateral chest walls and shoulders, limiting assessment of the chest wall, soft tissues, and left shoulder. The left basilar opacity cannot be definitively separated into consolidation vs collapse vs effusion on a single frontal film, and the etiology of the bilateral airspace disease (edema vs infection vs ARDS) cannot be determined from the image alone. Pretrained model scores (DenseNet, PSPNet) come from PA-dominant training sets and were used only as corroboration; near-threshold classifier scores were not treated as findings.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph of a pediatric patient. There is a large confluent opacity occupying the right hemithorax (patient's right), extending from the mottled apex to the base and from the chest wall to the mediastinum, containing multiple rounded, thin-walled cystic lucencies (a 'bubbly' multicystic pattern) that are most prominent in the mid-to-lower zones. The right hemidiaphragm and right costophrenic angle are obscured by the opacity. The left lung is well-aerated and clear, without definite nodule, mass, consolidation, effusion or pneumothorax. There is no clear large contralateral mediastinal shift; the trachea is roughly midline (if anything slightly toward the right). A faint external lead/cable overlies the right lateral chest wall (artifact).
impression: A large right-sided pulmonary consolidation/opacity with multiple thin-walled cystic lucencies (pneumatoceles vs a multicystic congenital lesion) in a pediatric patient. Most consistent with necrotizing pneumonia with pneumatoceles, with a cystic congenital lesion (CPAM) as the main alternative.
limitations: Single portable AP view (cardiac magnification, possible rotation, suboptimal penetration); no lateral view and no cross-sectional imaging (CT) to definitively characterize the cystic lucencies (pneumatoceles vs congenital cysts) or exclude a loculated effusion. The patient appears pediatric, but the pretrained models used (anatomical segmentation and pathology classifiers) were trained mainly on adult chest X-rays and are off-distribution, so their outputs were used only as weak corroborating signals and never to establish a finding. The direction/magnitude of tracheal/mediastinal deviation is difficult to assess precisely on this film (hazy trachea, possible rotation). A faint external ECG lead/cable overlies the right lateral chest wall.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. Bilateral basilar- and mid-zone-predominant patchy/reticular pulmonary opacities (left more prominent than right), consistent with parenchymal infiltrates/consolidation/atelectasis. A small rectangular radiopaque metallic object with a thin lead projects over the right mid-lung (indeterminate: external monitoring device versus retained/implanted metallic foreign body). Multiple indwelling lines and tubes are present, including a looped catheter/drain overlying the right lower lung field and a wide-bore tube coursing down the midline from the neck. A radiopaque '8H' study marker overlies the left shoulder. No pneumothorax, no discrete pulmonary nodule or mass, no cardiomegaly, and no large pleural effusion identified.
impression: Bilateral basilar/mid-zone pulmonary opacities (infiltrates/consolidation, left greater than right) in a patient with multiple support devices; a focal radiopaque metallic object is present in the right mid-lung (indeterminate). Clinical correlation recommended.
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral), limiting depth localization and small-effusion assessment. The image is a processed 8-bit export (not raw DICOM), so intensities are windowed. Multiple radiopaque lines/tubes and a study marker overlap the lung fields, limiting evaluation of underlying parenchyma and confounding automated classifier scores (which were weak and mutually inconsistent). The nature of the metallic object (external device vs foreign body/implant) cannot be determined without clinical context. Bounding boxes for the zone-level opacities are approximate.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. A left intercostal chest tube/drain is in situ: a long, thin, radiopaque tube traverses the left hemithorax with its tip projecting over the left apex, coursing inferiorly and laterally (with a mid-course kink) to cross the left hemidiaphragm/chest wall in the lower zone, its external portion running off the inferior image edge. A second short (~5 cm), straight, radiopaque linear density overlays the left lower lung field, medial to and not clearly connected to the chest tube (identity uncertain - probable small catheter/drain or wire). Both lungs are otherwise well aerated without definite focal consolidation; the costophrenic angles appear sharp without large pleural effusion. No definite pneumothorax is identified on visual inspection (no clear visceral pleural line), although a small/residual pneumothorax cannot be excluded (see limitations). A radiopaque clip/monitoring device over the left shoulder and external ECG lead wires over the right chest are external artifacts, not intrathoracic findings.
impression: Left intercostal chest tube/drain in situ (likely placed for pleural drainage, e.g. pneumothorax or effusion); the lungs otherwise appear clear with no large residual pneumothorax, effusion, or consolidation identified on this single view. An additional short radiopaque line in the left lower zone is of uncertain significance (possible second small drain or wire).
limitations: Single frontal view without a lateral view. Overlying external monitoring devices (left shoulder clip, right-sided ECG leads) and the chest tube itself limit assessment; the left base and lateral costophrenic angle are partly obscured by overlying arm soft tissue. Model discrepancy: ResNet-512 flagged pneumothorax with high probability (0.92) but no definite visceral pleural line was identified on visual inspection and DenseNet-224 did not flag it (0.03), so a small/residual pneumothorax cannot be excluded. The identity of the short left-lower-zone radiopaque line is uncertain (could be a second small drain, a wire, or an external lead). 8-bit image with reduced dynamic range (max 216) limits fine pleural detail; no clinical history available.

findings: Portable AP supine chest radiograph of a critically ill patient. A tracheostomy tube is appropriately positioned in the midline trachea. Multiple ECG monitoring electrodes and several support lines/tubes are in situ. Bilateral basal opacities are present: hazy air-space opacity in the right lower zone with a curvilinear opacity (suggestive of a fluid-filled minor fissure / band atelectasis) and an obscured right hemidiaphragm; diffuse opacity in the left lower zone with an obscured left hemidiaphragm. A discrete, short, smooth, curved radiopaque rod/tube projects over the left lower hemithorax/upper abdomen (identity uncertain). Multiple looped/coiled catheters are present in the mid-chest over the mediastinum/left heart border. No definite pneumothorax. The cardiac silhouette cannot be reliably assessed (AP projection, obscured borders).
impression: Bilateral basal opacities in a critically ill (tracheostomized) patient, most consistent with pneumonia/consolidation, with possible superimposed pleural effusions and/or dependent atelectasis. Multiple support devices in situ, including a discrete radiopaque rod/tube of uncertain identity over the left lower hemithorax and looped mid-chest catheters. No acute pneumothorax.
limitations: Portable AP supine technique (cardiac magnification, low lung volumes, dependent layering of fluid); multiple overlapping lines/tubes and ECG electrodes obscure the lung fields and mediastinum; a black band artifact at the right image edge; single frontal view without a lateral, so effusion vs consolidation vs atelectasis cannot be fully distinguished; deep-learning classifiers (PA-trained) are partially out-of-distribution on this supine ICU film and were used as supportive evidence only. Basal-opacity box boundaries are necessarily generous because the opacities are diffuse with fuzzy borders.

findings: Pediatric frontal chest radiograph obtained in EXPIRATION. Bilateral lower-zone airspace opacification, right greater than left. Right lower lobe: confluent dense basal opacity (consolidation and/or pleural effusion, with a meniscus-like lateral border) with overlying patchy mid-zone alveolar consolidation. Left lower lobe: milder, hazy/ground-glass opacity. Upper lung zones are relatively aerated. No definite pneumothorax (apices clear). No definite rib fracture. Cardiac silhouette is partially obscured by the right-sided opacity; no convincing cardiomegaly.
impression: Bilateral lower-zone airspace disease, right > left, most consistent with pneumonia (right lower-lobe consolidation with a parapneumonic pleural effusion) and milder left lower-lobe involvement, on a pediatric expiration-phase film.
limitations: Single frontal expiration-phase view; no inspiratory or lateral comparator, so effusion vs consolidation/atelectasis cannot be fully separated and the expiration technique can exaggerate basilar density via vascular crowding. Pediatric expiration films are out-of-domain for the adult-trained models used: CheXpert-DenseNet weights showed uniform over-firing and were discounted, and the PSPNet right-lung mask failed (whole-image bbox) and was discounted; remaining models were used for pattern support only, not localization, and their scores are non-spatial and non-calibrated for pediatric data. Cardiac size is only partially assessable due to overlying opacity.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. There is a large, dense, homogeneous opacity in the right mid and lower hemithorax with a concave (meniscus) upper border rising laterally, obliterating the right hemidiaphragm and the right costophrenic angle - a large right pleural effusion, with an adjacent rounded dense medial component consistent with compressed/atelectatic right lower lobe. A thin right-sided chest drain (intercostal catheter) and two small ECG electrode clips overlie the right lateral chest wall (devices, not lesions). The left lung shows diffuse, patchy reticular/interstitial opacities centred perihilarly and in the mid-lower zone (mild pulmonary edema or early infection); the left costophrenic angle is sharp. The trachea and mediastinum are roughly midline without significant shift. The upper zones are clear, with no pneumothorax and no definite rib fracture. The right heart border is obscured by the effusion, so the cardiac size cannot be assessed.
impression: Large right pleural effusion with adjacent right lower lobe compressive atelectasis and a right-sided chest drain in situ; background diffuse interstitial/patchy opacities in the left lung. No pneumothorax or definite rib fracture.
limitations: Single frontal view; no lateral view, decubitus, or prior films for comparison. Digitized film with non-uniform contrast/vignetting. The patient's right arm is abducted (dark extra-anatomic gap at the image's left edge), which may introduce rotation and limits assessment of the right upper chest wall and mediastinal position. The effusion is dense/homogeneous (no internal detail, no definite air bronchograms), so the relative proportion of pleural fluid vs. parenchymal consolidation/atelectasis cannot be precisely separated. The right heart border is obscured by the effusion, so cardiomegaly cannot be assessed. The inferior and medial borders of the opacity blend into the diaphragm/upper abdomen and mediastinum, so the exact lower/medial extent of the bounding box carries ~10-20 px uncertainty. The left-sided opacities are diffuse/interstitial (non-focal) and were therefore described but not given a separate bounding box. Classifier outputs are whole-image, operating-point-normalized scores (not calibrated probabilities) without localization; the final box is based primarily on direct visual inspection with an overlay, cross-checked by the MedSAM dense-core mask.

findings: Bilateral lower lobe lung opacities consistent with effusion and infiltration. Enlarged cardiac silhouette (cardiomegaly) is visually apparent. Multiple medical devices present including an endotracheal tube, various tubes, and ECG leads.
impression: Bilateral pulmonary opacities and cardiomegaly, likely representing congestive heart failure with associated pulmonary edema and pleural effusion.
limitations: Quantitative cardiac metrics (CTR and cardiomegaly score) are unreliable due to identified software logic failures. Device localization was coarse, making specific identification of all hardware difficult.

findings: Bilateral lower zone opacities, highly suspicious for pleural effusions and/or consolidation/atelectasis. Cardiomegaly is present. Multiple medical devices are visible, including an endotracheal tube, central venous catheter, and ECG leads.
impression: Bilateral lower zone opacities and cardiomegaly in a patient with multiple life-support devices, consistent with congestive heart failure or bilateral pneumonia.
limitations: AP portable projection, which can exaggerate cardiomegaly. Suboptimal inspiration and overlying medical hardware may obscure some details.

findings: Single frontal (AP, portable/supine) chest radiograph of a critically ill, intubated patient. Bilateral hazy airspace and interstitial opacities, right greater than left, most prominent in the right mid-to-lower zone and the left base. The right heart border, right hemidiaphragm and right costophrenic angle are partially obscured. No pneumothorax is identified, and there is no definite focal lobar consolidation, mass or rib fracture. A radiopaque tracheal tube (endotracheal or tracheostomy tube) is present with its tip positioned high, in the upper trachea near the thoracic inlet. ECG electrodes and external monitoring lines overlie the chest. The lower hemithorax and upper abdomen are under-penetrated (over-bright).
impression: Bilateral hazy airspace opacities (right > left) in a critically ill, intubated patient, most consistent with pulmonary edema (cardiogenic or non-cardiogenic/ARDS) and/or bilateral pneumonia. Dependent atelectasis and small pleural effusions cannot be excluded. No definite acute focal abnormality (e.g. pneumothorax) is seen.
limitations: Single frontal (AP) view only; portable/supine acquisition with no lateral view and no prior for comparison. Under-penetration of the lower hemithorax/upper abdomen limits assessment of the hemidiaphragms, costophrenic angles and retrocardiac region. ECG electrodes and external monitoring lines overlie the lung fields. Cardiac size is difficult to assess on a supine AP projection. Pretrained pathology models disagree on cardiomegaly, effusion, atelectasis and mass, and the segmentation model could not delineate the hemidiaphragms; these features should be considered uncertain. The tracheal tube type and high tip position (upper trachea) should be confirmed clinically.
